The Legend of Zelda: Ocarina of Time remake has launched, and it's glorious. But the real challenge isn't saving Hyrule as Link; it's finding a restock of the Zelda 40th Anniversary Edition Nintendo Switch 2 console.
Restocks are rolling out — Target and Nintendo recently dropped fresh chances to grab the hard-to-find console — and with Nintendo promising more stock is on the way, I'm bringing you the latest stock updates.
As of now, there is no Zelda Switch 2 restock available . However, multiple retailers are prioritizing in-store restocks (Best Buy, Walmart, GameStop), so if you can, be sure to check your nearest locations.
I've been covering pre-order events and restocks at Tom's Guide for more than five years, and know how to secure in-demand items. Below are all the links you need, alongside live updates on Zelda Switch 2 restocks.
The Legend of Zelda: Ocarina of Time has been remade for the Nintendo Switch 2. One of the N64's most beloved games has been completely overhauled to celebrate the franchise's 40th Anniversary. The remake offers truly stunning visuals with 4K graphics, overhauled controls, and reworked puzzles.
I'm a Senior Entertainment Editor at Tom's Guide and a more recent convert to The Legend of Zelda series. Breath of the Wild on Switch 1 was my first Zelda experience, and I can't wait to finally play Ocarina of Time.
If you didn't know there are two versions of the cover art for the Ocarina of Time remake. One with foil texture and one without.
Apparently, the retails have all swapped out the foil cover on their listings for the standard edition.
You may get lucky if you try your luck in-store, but online it appears out of stock.
GameStop is showing the Zelda console as out of stock but the Pro Controller might still be available. However, the retailer has been pushing in-store so you won't be able to get it on the website.
I called my local GameStop and they were out of stock, but you might have better luck with your closest store.
I just did a sweep through the retailers, and it looks like the only thing available is the 40th anniversary Pro Controller for $213.99 at Walmart , which is double the normal $99 price, but cheaper than what I'm seeing on Best Buy (showing as sold out).
Nothing to report at present, Target has now returned to "sold out", though perhaps we'll see a third restock later today, meanwhile no signs of any stock at Walmart so the rumors are unfortunately looking increasingly unlikely. In-store remains your chance to find a Zelda Switch 2 , so if you live locally to a retailer, it's worth trying your luck. Meanwhile, my day is winding down, but I'll be handing over to a colleague shortly, to make sure you don't miss any restocks.
Quick update on the Target situation, I'm no longer seeing the "add to cart" button, but it does direct me to "show in-store stock" with at least one location popping up claiming to have stock nearby. It would seem all the online inventory has been snapped up, but I would still recommend checking for now, you could get lucky. And Target has restocked online twice now, could it go for a third?
I didn't see this one coming, but the "add to cart" button has just returned on Target, so get over there and see if you can secure a Zelda Switch 2 as it looks like stock is returning at the retailer!
All eyes are on Walmart at present, there are rumors flying around they will restock the Zelda Switch 2 today, but so far nothing. Remember, as I keep saying, there's no confirmation here, but restock rumors often prove to have some truth to them, so fingers firmly crossed the noise around Walmart amounts to a drop.
Well, after about an hour, I'm not seeing any signs of available stock at Target, even with a lot of refreshes, so I feel pretty confident saying the retailer is once again sold out . Hopefully you were able to grab one in this latest Zelda Switch 2 restock. If not, don't worry, I'm still here tracking stock levels across retailers. Remember, Walmart is rumored to drop next.
Target was the big one today, and after restocking in the very early morning hours, I wondered if that would be the retailer sold out again, but a second restock has appeared online. The console is going to sell out fast, so get over there, and even if you get a "sold out" message at first, keep trying, as more stock could appear.
No time for talking, the Zelda Switch 2 is IN STOCK at Target, go grab yours!!!
Last night after a busy day of restock tracking, I finally got to sink my teeth into The Legend of Zelda: Ocarina of Time, and while I'm very early in my quest, my first impressions are that it's a glorious remake.
Our reviewer, Anthony Spadafora, had a similar experience, calling it "even better than my childhood memories." You can read his full Ocarina of Time review if you're looking to fill some time until we have more restock news to bring you.
Rumors have been flying around this week that Walmart could restock the Zelda Switch 2 from November 6 (aka today). This is based on an unverified leak of an internal document suggesting that the national retailer was gearing up for a restock. Again, this is all unconfirmed, but it's the retailer to watch right now, and it has already this week restocked in-store, so could an online drop follow today?
One of the big themes this week has been retailers opting for in-store restocks rather than dropping stock online.
I've just checked some local Target stores, and the retailer's online tracker is telling me there is Zelda Switch 2's available at nearby locations. However it's very limited ("only 1 left"), and these in-store stock trackers aren't always updated in realtime, so even if it tells you there's stock there's no guarantees.
Still, if you've got your heart set on securing a Zelda Switch 2, and have a Target store within reasonable distance (I wouldn't recommend a lengthy roadtrip), then getting down to your nearest location might be your best chance of getting one.
It looks like Target opted for a late-night online restock based on what I've seen on social media, so if you're still on the hunt for a Zelda Switch 2, that's the place to check now. But I'm seeing conflicting reports, with some users claiming that no stock was available, so I'll keep watching the retailer for signs of more stock.
Good morning! Rory here, it's a new day, and I'm back online to track Zelda Switch 2 restock across retailers. Today (Nov. 6) is set to be a big day with at least one online restock confirmed at Target, and there could be more on the way, too.
Once more, Target had in-store pickup available today, but online orders for the Switch 2 console start tomorrow (Nov. 6).
Lets take another run through the retailers. As we wind down toward the end of the work day, I don't expect any updates.
I've seen a few reports indicating that Amazon is suddenly delaying Ocarina of Time pre-orders by nearly a week.
To put it mildly, people are not happy .

articles.title_orig: After cancer surgery, Pope Leo embarks on Latin America trip with a first stop in secular Uruguay
articles.title_zh: After cancer surgery, Pope Leo embarks on Latin America trip with a first stop in secular Uruguay
articles.content_orig:
Pope Leo is travelling to Uruguay, Argentina and Peru
Pope Leo XIV is beginning a lengthy trip to Latin America just three weeks after surgery for lung cancer - a tour that includes a much-anticipated "homecoming" to Peru where he was a priest for many years.
The Vatican says no extraordinary measures are being taken in relation to the Pope's health, describing him as a "71-year-old who has undergone an operation" not someone with a "permanent medical condition".
It was Leo himself who revealed last month that doctors had discovered a tumour during a routine scan. The growth was removed along with the lower lobe of his right lung and his medical team then confirmed the cancer had not spread.
At a briefing in Rome ahead of the trip, which takes in Uruguay and Argentina as well as Peru, a spokeswoman stressed that Pope Leo had "fantastic stamina" and was "extremely enthusiastic" about the schedule which he had "personally confirmed... with no changes".
"The Vatican's message with this trip is, 'that was a short episode and now we're back on track'," Professor Massimo Faggioli of Villanova University told the BBC, pointing out that the Pope has had a busy return to work since his surgery.
"We have seen him in these last few days making speeches, audiences and so on. He seems in great shape. That was important."
On Friday Pope Leo presided over the annual memorial Mass for cardinals and bishops who have died
The 12-day tour would be demanding for anyone, though. It incorporates multiple long-haul and local flights and covers thousands of miles from the Amazon to the Andes.
The starting point will be Uruguay, where the number of Catholics has fallen away steeply in recent years and which is getting its first Papal visit in four decades.
Leo then heads for Argentina, homeland of Pope Francis, his predecessor.
Father Fernando Laguna said his heart was filled with joy when the Pope's visit to Argentina was announced
"This visit is also a homage to Francis, who didn't make it to Argentina [as pope]," says Father Fernando Laguna, the rector of Santa Maria Addolorata, Argentina's national church in Rome.
"When this visit by Pope Leo was announced, it filled all of our hearts with joy," he told the BBC. "I always thought he would go, despite his illness. I don't think he ever thought of calling it off!"
The priest is installing a big screen inside the church in Rome to allow parishioners to follow all the key moments of the trip from afar. The building is already decked out with posters declaring Pope Leo is welcome in Argentina. "We're waiting for you!", one proclaims.
'Welcome Pope Leo' reads this poster in the Argentinian church in Rome
This leg of the Pope's journey - which includes meetings with heads of state as well as religious events - could be the most politically sensitive. President Javier Milei once called Pope Francis "evil on earth" and a "communist" for promoting a doctrine of social justice to help the poor. In turn, Argentina's bishops have criticised Milei's harsh austerity measures, making sweeping cuts to social spending.
But Milei has already welcomed Pope Leo, writing in a post on X that Argentina awaits "with immense joy". Millions are expected to turn out to greet him.
The highlight of the trip is undoubtedly saved for last, when Pope Leo reaches Peru - described by the Vatican as a return to his roots.
"He knows these streets," is how a spokeswoman put it.
Worshippers at Chiclayo cathedral in Peru were delighted when their former bishop became Pope in 2025
Born in the US, the then Robert Prevost spent almost 20 years in Peru, on and off, and even has Peruvian citizenship. That time is seen as fundamental to shaping his papacy.
His schedule includes a return to the diocese of Chiclayo where he was ordained bishop in 2014 and remained until Francis moved him to the Vatican almost a decade later.
He will also travel to Cusco, former capital of the Inca Empire, to say Mass more than 3,000m above sea level before heading to Pucallpa in the Amazon.
In all three countries, the Vatican says the Pope will have meetings with survivors of clerical sexual abuse - an issue which clouded a 2018 visit to Chile and Peru by his predecessor.
"This is how the papacy reconnects with Latin America after Francis, whose visits to the region were not always seamless," is how Professor Faggioli sees it.
He believes Pope Leo has a strong sense of the unity of the Americas as one continent. "Democracies are in trouble there, so there are so many things he can address," he suggests.
"The big question then is the United States. There's no question he wants to go. So will he travel when [President Donald] Trump is still in office? I'm sure they're thinking about this."

articles.title_orig: ChatGPT ‘manipulated and encouraged’ a woman in her plot to poison her husband, suit alleges
articles.title_zh: ChatGPT ‘manipulated and encouraged’ a woman in her plot to poison her husband, suit alleges
articles.content_orig:
A North Carolina man sued OpenAI, alleging that ChatGPT gave his estranged wife detailed instructions on how to poison him.
James Gates, of Charlotte, said he fell severely ill in July 2025 but recovered. He later found a note handwritten by his wife, Cheryl Harris Gates, that referred to the plan and included a reminder to delete her ChatGPT history, the civil lawsuit says.
The suit, filed in October in San Francisco Superior Court, alleges the chatbot is “defective” and “manipulated and encouraged” Harris Gates to poison her husband. It says Gates suffers from severe physical and emotional harm.
An OpenAI spokesperson said “safety is a top priority” and that Harris Gates was banned from the platform. The company said it works with mental health experts to help ChatGPT recognize signs of distress and to expand access to localized crisis resources and hotlines.
Harris Gates was arrested in October 2025 and charged with attempted murder and contaminating food or drink with a controlled substance. The district attorney’s office later dropped the charges for lack of evidence.
An attorney for Harris Gates declined to comment.
According to the lawsuit, Harris Gates began using ChatGPT in early 2025  to assist with work evaluations. She was then employed by Charlotte-Mecklenburg Schools and her husband worked in cybersecurity.
By summer, the suit says, she relied heavily on the chatbot for children’s activities, gardening and appearance advice, and household questions. She eventually began sharing her frustrations about her marriage.
“During this same period the couple’s marriage had come under increasing strain, primarily driven by finances,” the suit says. The couple had discussed divorce, but Gates had not contacted a divorce attorney.
The lawsuit alleges ChatGPT validated Harris Gates’ frustrations and began “feeding Cheryl’s increasing mistrust and delusions about her husband spying on her and planning to leave her and her kids with nothing.” Gates had told his wife he never intended to do that, the suit says.
Over several conversations, Harris Gates allegedly portrayed her husband as “narcissistic” and “controlling.” She is also accused of asking for details “about how to poison her husband, including what dosages and drugs to use and combine for his weight,” and how to conceal the purchases from law enforcement.
In one exchange, the suit alleges, she asked about the toxic plant oleander and inquired about how many leaves would be lethal. She allegedly framed her questions “as self-protection,” saying she feared her husband would poison her with it. ChatGPT responded with specific instructions on preparation, dosage and administration, and whether the plant would show up on an autopsy, the suit alleges. It says the chatbot also told her the plant’s bitter taste could be masked in her husband’s energy drink.
In another exchange, the suit says, Harris Gates asked if mixing  Ambien and pregabalin “is better hidden in a beer at night or Celsius in the morning.” The chatbox allegedly said the energy drink would be better and then made a table “rating which drinks best mask the taste of the poisons.”
The suit further alleges she asked which combinations and doses of drugs already in the home could be made lethal, and that ChatGPT told her how to deliver them. It also alleges the chatbox named local places where she could anonymously buy castor beans, the main source of ricin.
During the July 2025 incident, Gates said, he had a racing heart, extreme jitteriness and uncontrollable shaking. His symptoms were so severe that he could not leave his couch for days, the suit says.
A month later, according to the suit, Gates recorded a video of himself pouring his energy drink into a cup after leaving it open on the kitchen counter while his wife was home. He wanted to see if anything was in it  but noticed nothing. The video was later given to police.
Gates told USA Today that his wife moved in August 2025. He said he found the handwritten note after she came to pick up her belongings and left a notebook on the kitchen counter. When he picked it up, the paper fell out.
The suit alleges that Harris Gates’ Amazon history showed searches for syringes. Liquid droppers, syringes, a scale and gloves were found at the home during a police search, it says. It also accuses ChatGPT of prompting her to delete her chat history so it cannot be accessed, even if subpoenaed.
Gates’ lawsuit says OpenAI was negligent and seeks unspecified damages. He told USA Today that he is separated from his wife and has temporary custody of the children.
Minyvonne Burke is a senior breaking news reporter for NBC News.

articles.title_orig: The Taipei Mayor Election Is Not About China - The Diplomat
articles.title_zh: The Taipei Mayor Election Is Not About China - The Diplomat
articles.content_orig:
In October, well-known Taiwanese television host Kevin Tsai, popular on both sides of the Taiwan Strait, was spotted by the media attending a campaign event for Puma Shen, a legislator running for mayor of Taipei. Given Tsai’s popularity in China, his appearance quickly sparked criticism. The incumbent Taipei mayor, Chiang Wan-an, helped defuse the controversy by inviting Tsai to the opening of his own campaign headquarters. Three weeks after attending Shen’s campaign event, Tsai publicly stated that he had never supported Taiwanese independence and that his work required him to interact with people holding a range of political views. The following day, he attended Chiang’s campaign event.
If attending a rally is tantamount to declaring one’s support for Taiwan’s future, imagine what will be made of the November 28 vote.
Shen, the candidate of the ruling Democratic Progressive Party (DPP), has spent years studying Chinese influence operations and promoting civilian preparedness in Taiwan. Chinese authorities have opened an investigation into him on allegations of secession. Chiang, the Kuomintang (KMT) incumbent, has maintained an open channel of communication between officials in Taipei and Shanghai. Beijing and Washington may be tempted to interpret a Shen victory as a vote for independence or a Chiang victory as a turn toward China. Either interpretation, however, would link a municipal election to an issue that Taipei’s voters have not been asked to vote on.
Consider an exchange during the October 31 debate between Shen and Chiang. Chiang challenged Shen to explain why two redevelopment projects, one in Datong and the other in Neihu, had stalled. Chiang attributed the delays to restrictions on building heights near Taipei’s Songshan Airport. Shen fired back with a question of his own: If city officials knew about these restrictions, why hadn’t they explained them to residents from the outset? Chiang used the exchange to question his challenger’s command of city affairs. Shen, in turn, used it to ask what good that expertise did residents if they learned about an obstacle too late to do anything about it.
The most important takeaway from their heated exchanges, however, is not what the candidates said, but what they left unsaid. China, the elephant in the room when it comes to cross-strait relations, was not raised even once as a key issue during the two-hour debate.
That encapsulates the kind of local issues Taipei voters will actually base their decision on. Some might vote for Chiang, crediting him with moving other difficult projects forward, including one at Nanjichang Night Market. Others might favor Shen’s proposal to screen older buildings for earthquake risks and to help residents arrange repairs. Two homeowners could vote for different candidates – while holding precisely the same views about China. The election night count offers no way to tell.
Taipei’s recent electoral history illustrates the limits of interpreting local elections through the lens of national politics – and vice versa. In 2022, the city elected Chiang as mayor. Just over a year later, in the presidential election, the DPP’s Lai Ching-te carried Taipei, edging out the KMT’s Hou Yu-ih by just 641 votes. Chiang’s mayoral victory would therefore have been a poor guide to the city’s presidential preferences. There is even less reason to interpret a vote in the capital as evidence of a broader change of heart across Taiwan for or against a political party – or that party’s approach to China.
True, the result will shape national politics. Winning Taipei would give Shen a larger audience for his work on civilian defense. A second term would give Chiang greater standing within the KMT to make the case for engagement with Shanghai, and possibly Beijing. Plus, the Taipei mayorship has in the past served as a launching pad for presidential ambitions. Winning office gives a politician the chance to advance causes that may have had little to do with why voters chose him.
The election’s outcome could certainly also influence cross-strait relations. During Chiang’s tenure, the Taipei–Shanghai Twin-City Forum has kept officials from the two cities in contact. A Chiang victory would give him another term to pursue those exchanges. A Shen victory would test the conditions under which they can continue. Although Shen has criticized the forum’s value, he has said he would attend if it offered practical benefits and came without political preconditions. On October 14, Beijing’s Taiwan Affairs Office dismissed his offer, citing his alleged support for independence.
Suppose Shen wins, repeats his offer, and finds Shanghai unwilling to meet with him. Concluding that Taipei voters chose to sever contact would erase Beijing’s role in the decision. The reverse inference – that vote for Chiang implies approval of his engagement with Chinese officials – would be equally questionable. A Taipei resident might value Chiang’s ability to keep municipal officials talking while still opposing closer political ties. Wanting the conversation with Shanghai to continue is entirely compatible with wanting Beijing to have less say in Taiwan’s affairs.
Local governance is undoubtedly important for the stability of the Taiwan Strait. Taipei’s city government, for example, helps residents prepare for an air raid, down to practicing how to reach shelter when the sirens sound. How well the city carries out that work matters regardless of which party holds power. Still, it’s not going to be an issue that is top of mind when Taipei residents fill out their ballots.
On November 28, Taipei’s voters will choose who takes responsibility for the safety of their homes, the city’s readiness for an emergency, and its dealings with Shanghai. Beijing and Washington have good reason to pay close attention to what the next mayor does with that authority. But anyone claiming a mandate for independence or unification is looking for evidence the mayoral count cannot provide.

articles.title_orig: Anatomy of a Selloff: Sudden Chain Reaction Rattles Wall Street
articles.title_zh: Anatomy of a Selloff: Sudden Chain Reaction Rattles Wall Street
articles.content_orig:
Retail traders dumped the most stocks in a single day since the Covid pandemic, amid Thursday's massive tech selloff, according to Vanda Research.
Retail investors sold a net $338 million of single stocks on Thursday, with not even an hour into the close, which the market research firm noted was the largest one-day outflow since March 2020 for a group that has been known to buy the dip and keep cash within the market.
The selling comes amid a massive stock market drawdown as traders rotated out of technology. On Thursday, the Dow Jones Industrial Average plummeted 1,800 points, effectively erasing any post-midterm bump, while the Nasdaq Composite dropped into a correction.
"On a typical sell-off, retail buy the dip," read a note from the firm. "Today, that bid has effectively disappeared from individual names."
The firm noted that what buying remained has been concentrated in leveraged vehicles such as the ProShares UltraPro QQQ (TQQQ), which delivers three times the performance in the Nasdaq-100 index, and the Direxion Daily Semiconductor Bull 3X Shares (SOXL), which is supposed to track moves in semiconductors.
"This looks like a rare buyers' strike colliding with forced selling," read the note.
— CNBC's Nick Wells contributed to this story.
(Correction: Fixes day of the week in first paragraph.)

articles.title_orig: Protesters break into Microsoft data center site in Amsterdam as Europe’s backlash spreads
articles.title_zh: Protesters break into Microsoft data center site in Amsterdam as Europe’s backlash spreads
articles.content_orig:
Several hundred activists opposed to the construction of a Microsoft data centre in Amsterdam occupied the site on Friday, responding to a call for a two-day protest across Europe.
The collective Geef Tegengas, which campaigns for climate and justice, and the environmental group Fossielvrij entered the construction site in the Sloterdijk district, halting work for the day.
"It's so many things, so many struggles that come together in this data centre," Geef Tegengas spokesman, Nathan Timmer, told AFP.
"This thing will use as much energy as all of the households in Amsterdam combined... this thing will use a ridiculous amount of water."
Timmer, 30, also argued that the centre would be used "to facilitate AI warfare" and what he called the "genocide" in Gaza.
The activists made it on to the site by scaling barrier fences despite a police presence.
Once inside they shouted political slogans and sprayed anti-Microsoft messages on walls under construction.
Dutch news agency ANP reported that police arrested between 150 and 200 protesters. Other activists quit the site voluntarily.
AI data centres require large amounts of electricity -- placing increased pressure on grids often still reliant on fossil fuels -- and, in many cases, water to cool down hot computing equipment.
A backlash is growing worldwide against their environmental impact, and there are also concerns over noise, pollution, their appearance and how many jobs the facilities actually create.
A coalition of campaign groups called "Stop Dirty Data Centers" has been pushing for a pause in the construction of such sites and called for action on Friday and Saturday in European countries.
Microsoft did not immediately respond to a request for comment.

articles.title_orig: To Cross the Red Sea, Shippers Email Houthi Rebels. Read Their Inbox.
articles.title_zh: To Cross the Red Sea, Shippers Email Houthi Rebels. Read Their Inbox.
articles.content_orig:
Captains who wish to transit the Bab al-Mandab Strait have been using a communication channel with the Iran-backed Houthi terror group via email for safe transit, the Wall Street Journal reported on Friday.
While technically the Houthis have said ships not linked to the US, UK, or Israel are allowed through the strait, after the Houthis declared a maritime blockade of Saudi Arabia in July, shippers have begun emailing the terror group to receive assurances of their safety.
Emails are sent to an administrative entity established by the Houthis in early 2024 called the Humanitarian Operations Coordination Center, which handles applications and communicates the Houthis actions.
Emails seen by the WSJ show vessels stating that neither the ship nor the crew has any connections with Israel, the US, or the UK.
Ships will share their estimated schedules and assure that they will adhere to the International Regulations for Preventing Collisions at Sea.
If the Houthis reply, they will typically do so within the next 24 hours, the WSJ wrote, citing crew members and emails.
In one instance, the Houthis sent authorization to the Chinese containership Zhong Cheng Chang Ling, issuing it a one-week permit and telling it to keep its Automatic Identification System, which broadcasts a ship's identity, position, speed, and destination, in operation through transit.
Additionally, the ship was told to keep VHF Channel 16, a marine VHF radio frequency designated as an international distress frequency, in operation.
The email ends with an invitation to call the HOCC hotline number if needed and to subscribe to the HOCC email alert service to receive news and updates from the Houthis.
The official guidance from international maritime authorities is that vessels should not engage or register with the HOCC, and many vessels choose not to contact them, the WSJ wrote.
However, the captain of the Zhong Cheng Chang Ling told the WSJ that the ship management told him to contact the Houthis as an extra precaution.

articles.content_orig:
Buy One Founder Summit Ticket, Get a Second for Free. Register now.
Founder Summit begins Nov. 4, 9:00 a.m. ET. Get your pass savings & deals before it starts. REGISTER HERE.
Meta recently launched its Muse agents — a new generation of cuddly agentic helpers. Now, the company has launched Spaces, a new way to communicate and collaborate with them.
As far as I can tell, Spaces are basically breakout conversations that revolve around a particular topic — although Meta refers to them as “custom experiences.” They live in the sidebar of the interface where you interact with your Muse agent. Clicking on the Space brings up the conversation, where Muse works toward a particular goal on your behalf.
For instance, if you wanted to plan a vacation, you could open a new Space focused on that particular project, and whenever you want to work on it with Muse, you would click to open that particular tab. Or, if you’re focused on collecting recipes for an upcoming family event, you’d open a new Space for that particular project. Other examples Meta gives are a holiday gift tracker, a wedding planner, or a space for DIY projects.
“Describe an idea in chat, and Muse builds a space for you, whether that’s a tracker, a planner or a project board,” Meta says.
Spaces can also be easily integrated with third-party apps and information, Meta says.
“Connect the apps you use, and your spaces keep themselves up to date in the background, so new concert dates, price changes, or savings progress show up without you having to ask,” the company says.
On Friday, Mark Zuckerberg, Meta’s founder and CEO, posted about the new feature on X: “Playing around with spaces in Muse lately — tell Muse what you need and it builds it. I’ve made a BBQ game, an event tracker, and a home control dashboard. Excited to see what you build.”
Muse agents — and the cuddly avatars that enclose them — have been greeted with a relatively warm reception over the past few months. During its earnings call in October, Zuckerberg said that its agents had 10 million users in the U.S. and Canada — less than two months after the agents debuted.
The company is obviously busy building out the user experience around the agents. Spaces is actually the second new Muse feature that Meta has debuted over the last week. On Thursday, the company also announced Muse Voice , which allows users to video chat with their agent and give it commands verbally.
The company is in competition with other cute and cuddly AI agents — including OpenAI’s dots and SpaceXAI’s Grokbot , which were debuted with similarly cartoonish personas.

articles.title_orig: Could the US midterms put a pin in the AI bubble?
articles.title_zh: Could the US midterms put a pin in the AI bubble?
articles.content_orig:
Is the artificial intelligence (AI) gold rush coming to an end, or is this simply a reality check?
That's the question which is hanging over investors, and which has prompted steep falls on the world's stock markets.
The sell-off in the US on Thursday was most dramatic on the Nasdaq, home to tech industry titans such as Alphabet, Nvidia, Meta and Apple.
It followed sweeping gains by the Democrats in this week's midterm elections in the US, which have given the party full control of Congress.
A number of leading Democrats campaigned against the unhindered expansion of data centres, which have underpinned the growth of artificial intelligence.
Fears this will lead to more regulation of AI appear to have concerned investors. But worries about the industry's prospects have been growing for some time.
The release of Chat GPT by Open AI in late 2022 is widely seen as having generated massive public and corporate interest in the practical uses of AI. It also sparked a modern-day gold rush.
Investors flocked to put their money into companies producing computer chips and  networking infrastructure, building data centres and providing the energy to power them, as well as developing the AI itself. The value of tech companies soared.
The boom continued into this year. Investments in AI are expected to reach $1trillion in 2026 alone according to research by Goldman Sachs. The sector has scooped up so much available cash that other industries have seen their own borrowing costs increase as a result.
But investors want returns, and in recent months concerns have been growing about whether the AI boom can produce the expected riches.
Those worries have emerged at a time when public comments from AI researchers casting doubt over the safety of artificial intelligence - even suggesting it could represent an existential threat to humanity - have been grabbing headlines and fuelling speculation that a clampdown could lie ahead.
While the Trump administration has been all-in on AI, or "super intelligence" as the president likes to call it, many leading Democrats tapped into grassroots concerns about the expansion of data centres and their impact on local communities.
These were largely focused on the facilities' high consumption of water and electricity, which many feared would push up their household bills – as well as the noise, use of land, and general disruption associated with them.
A Gallup poll published in May showed 71% of Americans would oppose the building of a data centre in their community. The figure for a nuclear power station was 53%.
James Talarico, who won the Senate race in once staunchly Republican Texas, was one of those to respond to this scepticism.
"While we want to protect America's leadership in artificial intelligence, we are still grappling with how it will affect everything from how we work to how our children learn," he said.
"We must protect Americans and establish clear, consistent laws for businesses."
With control of both houses of Congress, Democrats are now expected to challenge the president's technology agenda more vigorously, while introducing legislation which could curb the expansion of the industry.
Texas' Democratic governor-elect Gina Hinojosa campaigned against data centres, pledging a moratorium on the construction of new facilities.
Hinojosa's win could present opposition to tech multi-billionaire Elon Musk, who has moved large parts of SpaceX and Tesla's operations to the state, for years a Republican stronghold.
The Tesla boss had spent nearly $450m to back Republican campaigns in the midterms.
As the co-founder of the British-based technology firm Arm Holdings, Tudor Brown, points out, "stock values are based on future earnings not present earnings". If the rewards are not likely to be as great as expected, some investors will choose to sell up.
The falls seen on stock markets over the past 24 hours would appear to have been triggered by the midterm results. But concerns that tech firms have become overvalued were being expressed long before the elections.
The question now is whether this is simply the removal of froth from an over-exuberant market, or a sign that the AI rush is a bubble about to burst, with much wider consequences.
Nandini Roy Choudhury of Future Market Insights thinks investors will assess whether the political shift could result in restrictions on data centre construction, energy consumption and the deployment of AI technology.
She adds there is unlikely to be an immediate widespread recovery in tech stocks as traders are likely to be more selective, favouring firms with stronger balance sheets.
Brown thinks the impact will be limited. Share valuations, he thinks, were inflated by expectations of "almost infinite AI growth", which have been followed by "a bit of a panic".
"There is a natural floor to this", he says. "After that it will reflect I think that actually there's still a lot of money being made in these companies".

The Trump administration announced last year that the tech broligarchâs space exploration firm would install its satellite internet service at the White House free of charge.
But four separate federal contracts now reveal that the Pentagon has since set aside almost $1.2 million for SpaceX to carry out similar-sounding work at the presidential complex, the Washington Post reports .
Elon Musk, Trumpâs sons, and many other Republican donors and contractors are likely to be probed.

It is unclear whether the deals relate to the internet services Trump officials previously said were a gift, or whether Muskâs company was expected to provide more than the initial package.
The Pentagon earmarked the money to support work at the White House Communications Agency, which manages comms systems for senior administration officials.
Nonprofit watchdog Democracy Defenders Fund identified the first three of the deals, worth a combined total of around $502,000, from public contracting data, while the Post later uncovered a fourth worth a further $686,000.

Muskâs company installing its equipment at the White House has already sparked security concerns among government comms specialists.
Members of his controversial DOGE cost-cutting drive reportedly turned up at the Eisenhower Executive Office Building last February to install the kit without having told the officials responsible for existing systems in advance.
Staffers said theyâd seen a network called âStarlink Guestâ pop up on their mobile devices around that time, though it was later removed.
At the time, administration officials told the New York Times that government lawyers had approved the donation.
âIâm very concerned,â Democracy Defenders Fundâs chief counsel Virginia Canter told the Post. âWe worry about pay-to-play access and these kinds of transactional arrangements.â
âWhen someone is given this access and subsequently given these government contracts, you have to wonder if these government contracts are in the best interest of the taxpayer,â she added.

articles.title_orig: AST SpaceMobile is so desperate for launch they're building their own rocket
articles.title_zh: AST SpaceMobile is so desperate for launch they're building their own rocket
articles.content_orig:
There are optimistic plans for spaceflight, and then there are optimistic plans.
AST SpaceMobile is a Texas-based, publicly traded company building very large satellites to provide direct-to-cell communications on Earth. But it has been having trouble finding rides to space. So on Friday, AST announced that it is developing a medium-lift rocket, named Blacklift, which will have the capacity to lift 20 metric tons to low-Earth orbit. Oh, and the company said it would start launching commercially in late 2028.
“The Blacklift rocket is the springboard to significantly expand our total addressable market, providing AST SpaceMobile with regular unconstrained access to orbit and providing for most favorable owner’s economics in the industry,” said Abel Avellan, founder, chairman, and CEO of AST SpaceMobile, in a news release.
To anyone with even a basic understanding of rockets, that timeline is wildly, fantastically, and stupidly optimistic. Still, the announcement is worth examining because it underscores two important trends in today’s launch industry.
First, it’s becoming increasingly apparent that satellite operators planning to deploy large constellations need to secure launch capacity years in advance, as Amazon did nearly half a decade ago. And if they can’t secure that capacity on favorable terms, they are now considering taking the extraordinary step of developing their own rockets.
And secondly, since investors are now recognizing the worsening launch crisis that Ars has been writing about for months, there is apparently capital to be raised for new entrants into the medium-lift launch market. AST is not the only company making fantastical claims of late. A firm called Cowboy Space said in October it was building a large rocket named Big Iron (full credit—that’s an excellent name) to launch orbital data centers. It also claimed its large rocket would make its first flight in 2028.
Let’s start with a little history. SpaceX became the first purely commercial launch startup to announce plans to build a new medium-lift rocket about two decades ago, in 2005. The company holds the record for the fastest time to orbit with the Falcon 9 vehicle, with a development time of 4.7 years.
But SpaceX had some significant advantages. By then, the company had been operating for more than three years, had extensive experience with the Merlin engine, and was less than a year away from its first launch of the smaller Falcon 1 rocket. In retrospect, it’s also clear that the company had an insanely talented team of engineers. Finally, the Falcon 9 was quite a bit smaller than the recently announced vehicles, Blacklift and Big Iron. In its initial form, Falcon 9 had a lift capacity of about 10 tons.
What about other companies? Since 2015, a number of other US companies—United Launch Alliance (Vulcan), Rocket Lab (Neutron), Relativity Space (Terran R), Firefly/Northrop Grumman (Eclipse), and Stoke Space (Nova) have announced medium to heavy lift vehicles, ranging in payload capacity from about 7 to 27 metric tons (Blue Origin’s New Glenn is much larger than any of these).
Of these, only Vulcan has reached orbit. It took 8.7 years, with an incredibly experienced launch team behind the vehicle and about $2 billion in aggregate federal support across its suppliers.
Broadly speaking, the track records of these existing launch companies suggest that developing a new medium- or heavy-lift rocket takes five to nine years from public announcement to first orbital launch. Moreover, many of these companies either started with smaller rockets or brought other valuable experience to bear.
AST SpaceMobile’s counterargument is that it won’t be starting from scratch. The company said Friday that it has signed an agreement with Firefly to deliver engines for the first three Blacklift rockets, provide engineering services over a three-year period, and acquire the perpetual license to manufacture the Miranda and vacuum-variant Vira engines from Firefly. Nine Miranda engines will power Blacklift’s first stage.
Yes, engines are typically the hardest part of a rocket’s development. And procuring Miranda engines will shave some time off Blacklift’s development. But it will probably be a year or two, not five. Procuring the Miranda engine—which likely remains at least two years from being tested in flight on the Eclipse rocket—does not eliminate the enormous engineering, manufacturing, testing, and regulatory effort required to develop a medium-lift rocket.
AST SpaceMobile is also paying a pretty penny for this privilege. It has committed $1.3 billion to Firefly for the engine license ($800 million), 27 Miranda engines and nine Vira engines ($250 million), and engineering support ($250 million). If we look just at the engine costs for a single Blacklift rocket, that’s $83 million per vehicle for the first three.
The bottom line is that AST SpaceMobile has made a launch timeline claim that is profoundly disconnected from the historical record of every comparable rocket development program this century. Maybe they’re a bunch of geniuses who will vibe-code the vehicle with Claude or Grok and shock us all.
More likely, though, is that this is a company that desperately needs to launch about 90 more of its massive BlueBird direct-to-cell satellites. Yes, the company has some existing commercial launch contracts with SpaceX, Blue Origin, and other companies. And in its news release, it said, “AST SpaceMobile will continue to use external providers, with agreements now covering in total over 100 BlueBird satellites to be deployed cumulatively between 2027 and 2028.”
But that raises an obvious question: If AST already has agreements covering the deployment of more than 100 BlueBird satellites by the end of 2028, what precisely is Blacklift supposed to accomplish? Do you spend several billion dollars to develop a rocket you don’t actually need?

articles.title_orig: Poised for breakout moment in Latin America, Pope Leo also faces test of health
articles.title_zh: Poised for breakout moment in Latin America, Pope Leo also faces test of health
articles.content_orig:
By Salvatore Cernuzio â Aboard papal plane
After Pope Leo XIV underwent lung surgery at Romeâs Gemelli Hospital, many doubted whether he would be able to travel to Latin America. The Pope, however, said he âwas convinced that this trip had to go forward.â
On board the ITA Airways flight at the start of his visit to Uruguay, Argentina, and Peru, he repeatedly expressed his happiness at being able to make the journey.
The itinerary spans 12 days, more than 30,000 kilometers, and 14 locations, with travel by car, plane, and helicopter, more than 50 engagements, and around 40 speeches.
An American Pope with a Latin American pastorâs heart, Pope Leo spoke proudly of his nationality and his right to vote in the US midterm elections.
He was happy to undertake this mission, he told the 82 journalists accompanying him from around the world, including ten from the countries he will visit.
He described it as the âmission of the Bishop of Rome, of the Pope,â âsharing the joy of the Gospel,â âannouncing the Good News,â and âwalking together with people, expressing that closeness which is so important for people, whether it be in their moments of joy or in their moments of sorrow.â
About an hour and a half after takeoff from Romeâs Fiumicino Airport, the Pope greeted the reporters, correspondents, and camera operators with a smile as they stood ready with their smartphones and equipment.
He began in three languages: â Buongiorno a tutti, buenos dias , good morning, everyone.â He then thanked them âfor your service, for the work that you do,â which is âso importantâ in helping to spread âGodâs message of peace and goodwill for all people.â
âI know some people were doubtful about this trip taking place,â Pope Leo said, reiterating his conviction that the journey should go ahead. He praised the Lord and thanked the medical staff accompanying him, saying he was in âfairly good shape.â
âSo, youâre the witnesses of that,â he told the journalists. âAnd Iâm happy that youâre joining us.â
The Pope also took the opportunity to formally introduce the new Prefect of the Dicastery for Communication, Maria Montserrat âMontseâ Alvarado, someone âthat many of you already know.â She had âjoined the Vatican team of the Holy Seeâ on November 1 to take on âthis challenging role as Prefect of Communications,â succeeding Paolo Ruffini, âwho has completed his term of service.â He praised her âwonderful experience,â âcreativity,â âlife and liveliness,â saying she would accompany them on the visit and help the Vatican and the Pope âin the very important dimension of communication.â
Before making his customary way down the aisle to greet the journalists individually, Pope Leo reiterated the priority of his sixth Apostolic Journey, namely to encounter the peoples and cultures of three Latin American countries and bring them âthe message of hope in todayâs world.â
Each country, he said, has âa very particular history,â with âmany things in commonâ and âmany differences.â
The longest part of the visit will be in Peru, a homecoming to the country where he spent more than 20 years as a missionary. It will include Chiclayo, the northern diocese where he served as Bishop.
Peru, he said, is âone of my many homes,â adding, âIâm very happy to be going back there.â
As he moved among the journalists, the Pope received books, letters, and gifts of all kinds, from a traditional Andean hat from Chulucanas, where his mission in Peru began, to a Chicago White Sox baseball.
As he signed the ball, he joked with the journalist who handed him the marker: âCareful, Iâve ruined other cassocks that way.â Asked where he found the strength to make the journey, he replied, âIn faith. The Lord is very generous to me.â He attributed his health to âgood doctors and a healthy lifestyle.â
Responding to correspondents from US news outlets who asked about the ballot he had mailed in for the midterm elections, Pope Leo said, âI have already made a statement about this. I am proud to be American and to exercise the right to vote.â
He explained that he had not voted in Peru, where he also holds citizenship, because there was no way for him to vote remotely. Had it been possible, however, he would have done so. âIt is a good thing,â he said.
Many of the questions concerned his health. One journalist asked if had he prayed about his illness at Lourdes during his visit to France. âAt that point there was no sign of any problems,â Pope Leo responded. âSurprisingly, in all the essential respects, everything was fine. I was much more concerned about the health of the people who were there.â
Asked what he now saw as an urgent priority for his pontificate following the operation, he replied, âA sense of commitment to continuing to be close to those who are ill, but I would also like to tell people that health care should be a right for everyone.â
He had a particular message for people with cancer: âDo not be afraid. Early diagnosis is the best approach, so regular checkups are a blessing.â
Pope Leo also said he had spent his stay at Gemelli reading âthe breviary, the prayer book, and the newspapers.â He said he has not yet returned to playing tennis: âNot yet, but I will.â
Turning to Ukraine, he commented on the truce in Oleshky that he had called for and worked to promote: âThank God for what has been achieved, but there is still much work to be done to achieve peace.â
Regarding the Argentine leg of the journey, the Pope described it as âa tributeâ to Pope Francis, âin the sense that I am visiting his country, which he was unable to visit,â while emphasizing that the priority is to visit this important country.
Asked whether he felt different, perhaps more at ease, when speaking Spanish, the language he learned during his missionary years, Pope Leo replied: âWait and see. Some people say there are significant differences.â
One of the more unusual gifts came from Eva Fernández, the Spanish correspondent for Radio COPE: a plaque for an imagined aircraft that could take him to the Camino de Santiago during the Año Jacobeo , the Holy Year of Santiago de Compostela, in 2027.
Pope Leo previously traveled the route by car before he was elected Pope. Spanish Catholics now hope he will return by plane, and as Pope.
Asked whether he would, he replied: âI would like to. What you want to do is one thing; what you can do is another.â

articles.title_orig: Everyone blames data centers for high electricity prices. But these are the real reasons.
articles.title_zh: Everyone blames data centers for high electricity prices. But these are the real reasons.
articles.content_orig:
Researchers estimate data center demand increased wholesale electricity prices 8.6% in the Arizona-New Mexico region, with a larger effect projected by 2028. Bipartisan federal legislation would change who pays for grid expansion.
Damien Willis, Organ Mountain News
LAS CRUCES - Data center demand increased wholesale electricity prices in the region encompassing Arizona and New Mexico by an estimated 8.6% during 2024 and 2025, according to new economic research that projects an even larger effect by 2028 as energy-intensive computing facilities expand across the Southwest.
The findings, published in a Federal Reserve Bank of Dallas working paper revised Oct. 9, provide a regional perspective on the growing debate over who pays for electricity infrastructure needed to serve large data centers.
On Thursday, U.S. Sen. Martin Heinrich, D-N.M., released a fact sheet explaining provisions of bipartisan legislation that would require data centers to cover the costs of transmission upgrades they create rather than shifting those expenses to existing electricity customers.
The research and legislation address different parts of the same economic problem: Growing electricity demand can increase the cost of generating power, while connecting large customers may require expensive new infrastructure.
The study, Processing Power: The Effect of Data Centers on Wholesale Electricity Markets , was written by economists Owen Kay, Robert Reaser and Reid Taylor.
Using an hourly model of electricity generation, demand and transmission across 23 U.S. regions, the researchers estimated how prices would differ if electricity demand from data centers were removed.
Their preferred scenario found that data centers increased wholesale electricity prices nationally by 6.9% in 2025.
For the Arizona-New Mexico region, the estimated effect averaged $2.93 per megawatt-hour, or 8.6%, during 2024 and 2025.
By 2028, the researchers project that data center demand could increase the region's wholesale electricity prices by $4.32 per megawatt-hour, or 14.7%, compared with a scenario without data center demand.
The projected national effect reaches 12.3% under the same assumptions.
These percentages represent modeled effects on wholesale electricity prices, not increases in household utility bills. The Arizona-New Mexico region also encompasses a broader electricity market, so the study does not establish a separate figure for New Mexico customers.
The research is a preliminary working paper, and its findings represent the authors' analysis rather than an official position of the Federal Reserve System.
One of the study's central findings is that the effects of data center demand are not necessarily confined to places where facilities operate.
Electricity moves between interconnected regions, allowing utilities and grid operators to obtain power from generators elsewhere when transmission capacity is available.
But when large data centers consume more electricity in one region, that power may no longer be available for export to neighboring markets.
The researchers found that California experienced substantial wholesale price effects partly because data center growth in the Northwest and Arizona-New Mexico region reduced the availability of lower-cost electricity that otherwise could have been exported.
The study also examined whether adding large electricity customers might lower rates by spreading existing infrastructure costs across more electricity sales.
That can happen when additional demand uses infrastructure already in place without requiring major new construction.
However, the researchers found that increased electricity generation costs can offset those savings. They also cautioned that large data center developments are likely to require new transmission lines, substations and other infrastructure, making the potential for lower retail rates more uncertain.
The study does not determine how much of the estimated wholesale price effects ultimately reaches individual household bills. Retail rates depend on utility expenses, contracts and regulatory decisions.
Heinrich's Bipartisan American Affordability and Jobs Act of 2026 would change how utilities recover the costs of serving major new electricity customers.
The legislation, introduced Sept. 30 , is sponsored by Heinrich and three other senior Senate committee leaders: Republicans Mike Lee of Utah and Shelley Moore Capito of West Virginia and Democrat Sheldon Whitehouse of Rhode Island.
Under the proposal, the Federal Energy Regulatory Commission would be directed to establish rules requiring data centers to pay for both their share of existing transmission infrastructure and additional upgrades needed to accommodate their electricity demand.
A separate provision would require new data centers and high-density computing facilities with electricity demand of at least 20 megawatts to cover incremental costs associated with the generation, storage, transmission and distribution infrastructure needed to serve them.
The legislation also would give states additional authority to establish rate structures for data centers and use certain revenues to reduce electricity costs for other customers.
Utilities would be required to report electricity sales to data centers through the U.S. Energy Information Administration, providing more detailed information about a rapidly growing category of electricity consumption.
In his Thursday fact sheet, Heinrich characterized the proposal as a way to prevent families and small businesses from subsidizing infrastructure built for large computing facilities.
The legislation has not become law, and its provisions would require additional regulatory action before taking effect.
An independent Nov. 3 analysis by the Bipartisan Policy Center examined how the legislation would allocate costs associated with data center expansion.
The analysis identified two distinct protections: requiring data centers to pay additional transmission costs alongside existing system charges and requiring large new computing facilities to cover the full incremental infrastructure costs associated with serving them.
It also noted that implementation would depend on federal rulemaking, state regulatory action and utility rate proceedings.
Those processes could take years, meaning any savings would not necessarily appear immediately on customers' monthly electricity bills.
The Bipartisan Policy Center also identified challenges in determining which infrastructure expenses are directly attributable to individual data centers and establishing rate structures consistent with federal and state requirements.
The research arrives as southern New Mexico confronts questions about the energy demands associated with Project Jupiter, the large data center development in Santa Teresa.
The project's proposed natural gas-powered energy facility is undergoing a separate state permitting process. On Thursday, Organ Mountain News reported that the developer had waived a previously contested air permit decision deadline and joined state regulators in seeking to postpone a December public hearing.
The Dallas Fed working paper does not estimate Project Jupiter's specific electricity costs or its potential effect on local utility rates.
The project also proposes substantial on-site electricity generation, making the distinction between electricity obtained from the grid and electricity produced independently important when considering the applicability of federal grid-cost requirements.
For New Mexico residents, the economic research establishes a broader concern: Data center expansion can affect electricity costs across interconnected markets, and those effects depend on where facilities operate, how much power they consume and whether additional generation and transmission capacity becomes available.
Heinrich's legislation addresses one part of that concern by proposing new rules governing which customers pay for grid infrastructure.

articles.title_orig: Jared Kushner’s European security plan isn’t convincing Europe
articles.title_zh: Jared Kushner’s European security plan isn’t convincing Europe
articles.content_orig:
BRUSSELS — Europe is once again watching the White House through gritted teeth.
An opaque Trump administration proposal for a new European-wide security arrangement with Russia has met skepticism from European capitals that fear it risks sidelining the continent and emboldening Kremlin chief Vladimir Putin.
“We already have a European security architecture in place — NATO and European Union both have their respective roles,” EU foreign policy chief Kaja Kallas said Friday in reaction to the U.S. plan. “We must make sure Ukraine is integrated into this architecture. The problem remains that Russia keeps breaking the treaties that underpin it ... Putin does not have a veto over European security.”
The latest U.S. proposal underscores growing anxiety around Trump’s fresh rapprochement with Russia as he ramps up pressure on Ukraine and his administration attempts to revive long-stalled talks to end Moscow’s full-scale war against Kyiv.
POLITICO spoke to 12 NATO diplomats, EU envoys and European government officials, all of whom were granted anonymity to speak freely on the sensitive issue. NATO allies were not briefed about the American plans in advance, according to three alliance diplomats, and many remain skeptical of the idea.
U.S. President Donald Trump late Thursday talked of a “big, beautiful agreement,” after meeting with Putin’s envoy Kirill Dmitriev, adding: “It’s going to involve more than Ukraine, and I could even say it might involve all of Europe.”
“Our objective is to develop practical arrangements that address the security concerns of all sides, reduce the risk of future conflict, and create a more stable and predictable security environment,” Trump’s son-in-law and envoy Jared Kushner added soon after.
Kushner said the arrangement would have five goals: “Permanent security consultations, reliable crisis communications, greater military transparency, reciprocal measures to reduce escalation risks, and an enduring framework for long-term European security and stability.”
“It is a bit obscure what Kushner meant,” said one NATO diplomat. “The general sentiment in Europe is that any discussion with Russia on the future architecture at the moment will just be used by Moscow to legitimize their arguments ... it will not fly with the European allies.”
A senior European official added: “Literally, there’s nothing to find fault with, but we know there’s something else going on.”
European Commission President Ursula von der Leyen’s top adviser, Björn Seibert, briefed EU ambassadors on Friday, according to two EU diplomats, following a discussion between national security advisers on the issue.
“There’s willingness to engage in Kyiv and in the rest of Europe although there’s little confidence in the Russians — but the EU is not blocking it,” one of the EU diplomats said after the meeting. But “the group around Trump underestimated how important the conflict is for Europe and how a bad outcome for Ukraine is very dangerous for Europe.”
“It's a long-standing position for us and many others that European security architecture should not be discussed while there is a war,” said a senior European security official. “And obviously not without Europeans.”
“Europe must have a seat at the table in negotiations on peace in Ukraine and the future European security architecture,” Lithuanian President Gitanas Nausėda added Friday, after a meeting of the eight Nordic and Baltic countries.
This week saw two rounds of working-level meetings in Brussels on a Ukraine peace deal, ahead of U.S.-brokered working-level talks with Ukraine and Russia on Nov. 10-11 in Abu Dhabi.
“We must be realistic about the peace talks and we must be very careful when it comes to the real intentions of Russia,” Polish Prime Minister Donald Tusk told a group of reporters, including from POLITICO, earlier this week. “In winter, Putin might have less incentives to get a deal.”
Stefan Kornelius, spokesperson for German Chancellor Friedrich Merz — who talked to Trump on Thursday night — said: “A new sense of urgency has ... emerged” on negotiations after this week's U.S. midterm elections, adding the issue would resurface at an informal gathering of EU leaders in Dublin next week.
The meeting had been intended to focus on AI, but developments in Ukraine could overshadow the talks, a third EU diplomat said. “Things are moving pretty fast,” they said.
Still, some allies fear the U.S. may tie its new initiative to an upcoming review of American troops in Europe, expected in December.
“That’s the elephant in the room,” said a second NATO diplomat. “One thing is talking about European security architecture ... with an ‘ordinary’ U.S. posture; another thing is to talk about a European security architecture ‘as things will be,’ and nobody knows how that’ll be.”

articles.title_orig: Bluetooth 7 Speeds Are Set to Quadruple in 2027, Especially for Audio
articles.title_zh: Bluetooth 7 Speeds Are Set to Quadruple in 2027, Especially for Audio
articles.content_orig:
Our expert, award-winning staff selects the products we cover and rigorously researches and tests our top picks. If you buy through our links, we may earn a commission.
Wireless tech is about to get a whole lot snappier. On Thursday, the Bluetooth Special Interest Group, the trade association that oversees Bluetooth, officially unveiled Bluetooth High Data Throughput, a flagship upgrade set to arrive as part of the Bluetooth Core 7.0 standard. The revision supercharges Bluetooth Low Energy by pushing maximum bit rates to 7.5Mbps, effectively quadrupling the throughput of the existing LE 2M technology. Compatible devices are slated to hit store shelves starting in 2027.
That’s good news for phone users , tablet havers , laptop groupies, smart speaker stans and more. Bluetooth is still the most popular medium-to-short-range wireless standard for connecting devices. But this is a big rollout, and the changes will start with premium wireless, such as earbuds, with other applications following.
Those other applications could include spatial computing, exchanging AI-related info with local devices, connecting to health wearables and a host of smart home applications, like playing Spotify through an Amazon Echo Studio or dimming a smart bulb .
“In practical terms, a smartwatch could sync hours of sensor-rich training data to a phone in seconds. A smart home product could complete a firmware update with little visible downtime,”  Damon Barnes, Director of Technical Marketing at the Bluetooth Special Interest Group, told CNET. “Smart glasses and other AI-enabled devices could exchange more data with a companion device or the cloud. And in audio, the additional capacity can support richer experiences, including high-resolution, lossless, surround, and spatial audio.”
A representative from the Bluetooth Special Interest Group didn’t respond to a request for comment.
The biggest change in this update is a new physical layer for Bluetooth. Layers are like different sections of the Bluetooth protocol, and the physical layer is the bedrock of the standard, the foundational layer involved in transmitting and receiving data signals.
Improvements in the physical layer can have very significant effects on all Bluetooth communications. In this case, new modulation schemes let the physical layer handle data more efficiently and transmit more data at once, which is why the speed increases are so significant.
These improvements also make the new standard more efficient, saving battery life in many applications. So your smart lock may last longer before you need to exchange the AA batteries, earbuds won’t need to go back in the case as fast, and so on.
We know the first flagship devices are expected to appear with the technology in early 2027, but don’t have an exact date.
Barnes also told use that since the update is starting with wireless audio, the first devices to see it will be headphones, earbuds and speakers.
With protocol changes like this, it can take some time for new products to reach the market, and manufacturers may take a long time, even years, to adopt it.

The office of Israeli Prime Minister Benjamin Netanyahu said Friday that aid provided by the U.S. has been used by Israel "both to defend itself and to confront enemies who threaten America and the West."
"U.S. military aid to Israel has always been a cross-the-aisle agreement," the office wrote on X after President Donald Trump announced earlier this week that $4 billion in aid would be "cut off at the end of the year."
"Today, Israel has a strong and stable economy. The move by PM Netanyahu and President Trump from aid to partnership shows the strength and sophistication of our relationship, and its ability to adapt and stand strong over time," Netanyahu's office added.
Trump said on Election Day, "Israel's our number one," and, "We give them more than anybody else, and they no longer need it."
President Donald Trump said Friday that "Israel and, in fact, the entire Middle East, WOULD NOT EXIST TODAY if I did not stop Iran from having a Nuclear Weapon.
"Nobody wants to say that, but everybody knows it’s true!" the president added in a post on Truth Social.
Trump made the remark after announcing earlier this week that $4 billion in U.S. aid to Israel would be "cut off" by the end of the year.
An Iranian military official vowed Friday that any country helping the U.S. in a potential new attack on Iran would become a legitimate target, a report said.
Brig. Gen. Ali Balali, who is a senior advisor to the commander of the Islamic Revolutionary Guards Corps (IRGC) Aerospace Force, also said Friday that Iran's missiles have enough range to strike U.S. and Israeli targets, according to Iran's Tasnim News Agency.
The remarks come after reports emerged last week that movements were being made in the Middle East to give President Donald Trump options if he decided to pursue further military action against Iran following Tuesday's midterm elections.
Russia played a larger role in the Iran war than previously disclosed, with internal defense industry documents revealing how Moscow built up the country's arsenal ahead of its conflict with the U.S.
A Russian contract is tied to 90 launchers for precision-guided missiles with the destination as Tehran, according to documents obtained and published by Ukrainian defense intelligence research group Dallas Analytics offering new details on the extent of Moscow's military support for Iran before war erupted.
President Donald Trump has repeatedly downplayed Russia's role in the conflict — as recently as last month, saying that he did not believe they are helping Iran "at all."
Russian production records show components were allocated for 90 APU-L twin-rail launchers under a contract identified as "K-10," with shipments within the Russian production chain scheduled from late 2024 through December 2025.
Other internal Russian documents obtained by Dallas Analytics explicitly identify "K-10" as Iran. An October 2022 supply request for equipment for a Yak-130 aircraft lists the consignee as "'K10' Iran" and was countersigned by the acting head of the Russian Defense Ministry's 704th Military Representation.
The United Kingdom Maritime Trade Operations Centre (UKMTO) said Friday that eight ships have been attacked so far this week in the Strait of Hormuz.
Since July 6, a total of 63 of 88 projectile strikes happened along a southern route near the coastline of Oman, according to the UKMTO.
There were also three ships attacked this week in the Arabian Gulf, it added.
"Of the 11 incidents, 3 continued their voyage, 5 required assistance and 3 Vessels sunk," the UKMTO said in a weekly overview, noting that the risk for ships traveling through the Strait of Hormuz remains "severe."

"Pete Hegseth, cabinet secretaries shouldn't be wasting taxpayer dollars on campaign style videos. Kristi Noem learned that the hard way," Tillis said in a post on X Friday.
"This is about you: the incompetence you’ve displayed, the bad advice you’ve given to the president, and your shameful and embarrassing episodes from firing our top generals to texting war plans to reporters," he added.
Tillis previously has called on President Donald Trump to replace Hegseth.
Ali Akbar Velayati, an advisor to Iran's supreme leader on international affairs, said Friday that, "Any energy or transit corridor that tries to bypass us will either become too expensive or unstable."
"Now that everyone is talking about the new order of West Asia, it should be noted that: Iran is a bridge between [the] Persian Gulf, Central Asia, Caucasus, and the Sea of Oman," he added on X.
"The domino effect of crises from Gaza to the Red Sea, and from Lebanon to Iraq, has shown that regional security is indivisible," Velayati said. "Either collective security is achieved, or everyone experiences collective insecurity."
“The tsunami of geopolitical changes in West Asia has engulfed the elections in Israel and the United States. The result: ‘Iran is now one of the principal architects of the regional order — a reality that can neither be eliminated nor replaced’,” Velayati also was quoted as saying Friday by Iran's Tasnim News Agency.
Vice President JD Vance privately accused Israeli Prime Minister Benjamin Netanyahu of being "wrong on everything" about the Iran war, according to reports, as disagreements over the conflict expose tensions within the Trump administration and raise questions about Vance's potential 2028 presidential ambitions.
The clash, reported by Axios Nov. 4., comes after Republicans lost control of both chambers of Congress in Tuesday's midterm elections and Vance publicly blamed the war for the party's defeat while urging President Donald Trump to pursue a negotiated settlement rather than renewed military strikes.
"The reason we lost is the war," Vance wrote later on Wednesday on X.
"Low-level hostility between Vance and Netanyahu is beneficial for Vance," Natan Sachs, a senior fellow at the Middle East Institute, told Fox News Digital.
"It allows him to give some distance from the Trump administration, which has just taken a huge electoral beating, but also to position himself ... in a very different position than President Trump himself without attacking Trump."
Qatar said Friday that President Donald Trump called its leader Sheikh Tamim bin Hamad Al-Thani to discuss "the ongoing diplomatic efforts aimed at de-escalating tensions in the region."
The state-run Qatar News Agency said Al-Thani and Trump "discussed the latest international efforts, notably the initiatives led by the State of Qatar, to bridge the gaps between the concerned parties and support the negotiation process, to pave the road for reaching a comprehensive agreement that resolves the crisis and ensures security and stability in the region."
The call comes as Qatar is acting as a mediator in talks between the U.S. and Iran that are aimed at ending the war.
Qatar said Al-Thani also "emphasized the importance of continuing dialogue and embracing diplomacy as a means of resolving disputes; preventing further escalation in the region; and safeguarding freedom of maritime navigation and the security of energy supplies."
The United Kingdom Maritime Trade Operations Centre (UKMTO) said Friday that a tanker ship traveling through the Strait of Hormuz reported an explosion.
The incident happened Thursday about 16 nautical miles east of Khasab, Oman, the agency said.

articles.title_orig: Apple Says More Than 100,000 Apps Optimized for iPhone Duo, Here's What's Still Missing
articles.title_zh: Apple Says More Than 100,000 Apps Optimized for iPhone Duo, Here's What's Still Missing
articles.content_orig:
Apple today announced that more than 100,000 apps have been optimized for the iPhone Duo, released two weeks ago. We confirmed that this figure refers to apps built with the iOS 27.1 SDK or later , meaning these apps fill the full width of the iPhone Duo's inner and outer displays and have vertical controls in the status bar.
A statement from Susan Prescott, Apple's Vice President of Worldwide Developer Relations:
It's been wonderful to see how quickly developers have embraced iPhone Duo, and we're grateful for their creativity and innovation. Today there are well over 100,000 apps built for iPhone Duo already live on the App Store, and thousands of optimized apps are being added to the store each day. In the last month alone, thousands of developers have joined us for workshops in 19 cities around the world to experience iPhone Duo firsthand and bring updated apps to their users. The enthusiasm has been incredible, and we're excited to see the pace of updates continue to accelerate as more and more apps optimize for iPhone Duo.
Apple said thousands of apps optimized for the iPhone Duo are being added to the App Store each day, with recent examples including Microsoft's Excel, OneNote, PowerPoint, and Word apps , along with the Etsy, Goodnotes, Halide Mark III, NBA, NHL, and Zoom apps. Other apps optimized for the device include Amazon Prime Video, Fantastical, Flighty, Instagram, MLB, Netflix, SmartGym, WhatsApp, YouTube, and more. There are too many to list.
Apps optimized for the iPhone Duo have a "Made for iPhone Duo" badge in their App Store listings on the device, making them easy to identify.
iOS 27.2 added Apple Pencil (USB-C) support to the iPhone Duo , enabling users to draw in apps like Procreate Pocket, take notes in Apple Notes, Fineliner, and TypeDraw, and mark up documents in apps like Preview on the device.
On the other hand, with millions of apps available in the App Store, there are unsurprisingly many apps that are still not optimized for the iPhone Duo, with the following examples listed in alphabetical order: AMC Theaters, Amazon Fire TV, Apple Store, Best Buy, Bluesky, Delta, DoorDash, Duolingo, Fandango, FedEx, Goodreads, Google Docs, Google Home, Google Sheets, Google Slides, GrubHub, JetBlue, Libby, Microsoft Authenticator, Microsoft Teams, MTA, Nike, PayPal, PictureThis, Ring, Southwest, Spectrum TV, Starbucks, Steam, Uber Eats, UPS, USPS, Venmo, Verizon, Wells Fargo, Whole Foods, and YouTube Music.
Apple said developers can easily optimize their apps for the iPhone Duo. Apps that use standard SwiftUI and UIKit components adapt automatically to each display, with controls moved to the status bar and multi-column support on the inner display. New APIs let developers optimize their apps for the device's various layouts and poses.
Apple has hosted more than 50 in-person iPhone Duo app workshops in 19 cities worldwide, and there are online resources like the Apple Developer Forums .
In the meantime, apps built with the iOS 27 SDK resize to fill most of the inner display on the iPhone Duo, but they avoid the status bar on the right edge. Apps built with the iOS 26 SDK or earlier run on the iPhone Duo, but appear in the center of the inner display, with lots of empty black space on the left and right sides of the apps.
iPhone Duo app optimization has been a hotly debated topic on social media platforms, with some people pointing out apps that are not yet optimized and others saying the issue is overblown. It is clearly a mixed bag, with some apps optimized and some not. More apps are being updated by the day, though, so the situation is improving rapidly.
