articles.title_orig: Russia secretly bolstered Iran's missile arsenal before war with US, records uncover
articles.title_zh: Russia secretly bolstered Iran's missile arsenal before war with US, records uncover
articles.content_orig:
Russia has supplied Iran with 90 advanced missile launchers, reports have said, as Moscow confirmed its close relations with Tehran.
Russia agreed a deal in 2024 to supply Iran with 90 advanced missile launchers, the Financial Times reported on Friday, citing documents from a major Russian defence manufacturer.
The report came a day after a senior Iranian official visited Moscow to discuss expanding a defence pact signed last year, and illustrates that Russia continues to deepen relations despite seeking the support of the United States for its narrative concerning the war in Ukraine.
The launchers are designed to carry Russia’s light multipurpose guided missile, known as the LMUR or Izdeliye 305. The precision weapon, capable of striking moving targets, entered military service in 2022 and has since been widely used by Russian forces in Ukraine.
The weapons are built for Russia’s Mi-28 attack helicopters, which Iran already possesses. Al Jazeera was not able to confirm if the order has been delivered.
The reported deal illustrates the strengthened military ties between Moscow and Tehran since Russia launched its full-scale invasion of Ukraine in 2022.
Western intelligence officials warn the relationship has further deepened amid the US war in the Middle East, despite President Donald Trump’s recent claims that Moscow was doing “very little, if anything” to help Iran.
The details of the deal emerged a day after Russian President Vladimir Putin met top Iranian security official Mohsen Rezaei at the Kremlin. Rezaei delivered a message from Supreme Leader Ayatollah Mojtaba Khamenei during the visit, which was aimed at “further development of bilateral cooperation”, the Kremlin said in a statement released on Friday.
Iranian President Masoud Pezeshkian met with Putin in late October.
The two countries, both under heavy Western sanctions, have continued to pull closer together in recent years.
In January 2025, they signed a comprehensive strategic partnership treaty covering trade, military cooperation, science, culture, and education.
The treaty took effect in October of that year, but unlike Russia’s pact with North Korea, it does not include a mutual defence clause.
However, the deal to supply the helicopter-mounted launchers highlights that military ties continue to strengthen. On Saturday, Iranian army spokesman Mohammad Akraminia said Tehran had bought Russian Su-35 fighter jets.
Meanwhile, amid the war in Ukraine, Tehran has provided Moscow with ammunition, artillery shells, firearms, short-range ballistic missiles, helmets, and flak jackets. It was suspected to be supplying drones.
After meeting Putin on Thursday, Rezaei, the secretary of Iran’s Supreme National Security Council, said the talks had focused on security arrangements in the region, as well as Russia’s support for ending what he called the US “aggression” against Iran.
“Important regional issues were discussed with Putin and significant conversations took place regarding the post-war period and regional security arrangements,” Rezaei said.
The Kremlin reported that “further development … of the Comprehensive Strategic Partnership Treaty” was also discussed.
Analysts suggested to the FT that Russia is walking a fine line to make sure its support of Iran does not disrupt its other relationships, including with other Middle Eastern countries and the US.
“Russia still has certain red lines when it comes to its involvement in this war,” said Hanna Notte at the James Martin Center for Nonproliferation Studies. “Which is why the support it has provided to Iran is operationally helpful but is not the game changer in this war.”

articles.title_orig: AI stocks climb after trillions wiped from market values
articles.title_zh: AI stocks climb after trillions wiped from market values
articles.content_orig:
Shares in artificial intelligence and technology firms have been climbing following an enormous sell-off that wiped trillions of dollars off stock values.
The tech-heavy Nasdaq stock index opened higher following a market rout that began in the US on Thursday before spilling over to Asian and European markets into Friday.
Investors had been selling off tech shares in part due to concerns the Democrat victory in the midterm elections would mean slower artificial intelligence development.
However the latest US employment figures added to a mixed picture for American markets on Friday morning, with an unexpectedly strong 165,000 jobs added to the economy in September.
On Thursday, businesses closely linked to artificial intelligence development took a hammering on stock markets, particularly chip and semiconductor makers.
But the Nasdaq Composite bounced back slightly on Friday, up 1.4%, reversing some of its 5.5% fall.
The S&P 500, which tracks the share prices of the largest publicly-traded US companies, was up about 0.7%, while the Dow Jones Industrial Average was flat through the day.
Nvidia shed hundreds of billions in market value on Thursday after shares slid more than 9%, but recovered some of those losses on Friday, trading up more than 3%.
SpaceX and Tesla shares, which were also hammered on Thursday, saw mixed gains, up more than 8% and nearly 5% respectively.
Chipmakers AMD and Micron both dropped by more than 17% on Thursday, but AMD shares had risen by about 10% on Friday while Micron was up more than 5%.
However, stock markets in Asia and Europe fared worse on Friday.
The Kospi in South Korea closed down 6% on Friday, with shares in chipmaker SK Hynix plunging more than 10%. European markets also fell, with the main indexes in Germany, France and Spain ending the day down.
In the UK, the FTSE 100, which tracks the largest companies on the London Stock Exchange, declined 1.01%.
In addition to the recent market volatility, UK traders were also digesting the latest Bank of England decision to raise interest rates and the signal that another rate rise could be on the cards to curb rising prices.
Dan Coatsworth, head of markets at AJ Bell, said it had been a brutal week for markets, and the key question was whether the jump in the S&P 500 and Nasdaq would be sustained.
"While no-one knows what happens next, it's clear that we've just seen a significant shift in market sentiment," he said.
"Once investors have had the weekend to catch their breath, next week could give a clearer indication of whether the tech trade is going down the pan or fighting back."
The market fluctuations come after the sweeping Democrat victory in the midterm elections.
A number of Democrats campaigned for new rules and regulations for artificial intelligence (AI) and data centres, and the party has since won control of both houses of congress as well as key contests in states that have been part of the AI data centre race.
US President Donald Trump on Friday reiterated his supported for what he calls "super intelligence", saying only "foolish leadership" would "say no to the riches they bring".
However, there have also been concerns over whether the enormous amounts of money being spent on AI will pay off.
Russ Shaw, founder of global tech advocacy firm Tech London Advocates, said the election result was sending a message that a rethink was needed on AI.
"The incoming Congress is going to really focus on AI in a very dramatic way," he told the BBC's Business Today.
"I'm a big fan of AI, but I'm watching what these companies are doing, and they're not communicating effectively at all, particularly in the US, about what the benefits of AI are all about."
He said people were watching firms come into their communities and build data centres while their own energy costs were going up, and those companies "have to be better neighbours".
As well as the fallout of the midterms and the plunge in artificial intelligence stocks, US traders will also be digesting the latest jobs figures.
And those numbers were better than expected: US employers added 165,000 new jobs in October, well above the average monthly increase and more than double what analysts had expected.
Overall the unemployment rate, which counts the number of people who are out of work but actively looking for a job, eased slightly to 4.1% from 4.2% in September .
The Bureau of Labor Statistics (BLS) said the unemployment rate has remained in the narrow range of 4.1% to 4.3% since March.
Neil Birrell, chief investment officer at investment firm Premier Miton, said while the jobs figures may feel like second billing to the market movements they were still important.
"The US economy is running hard which may mean the risks the markets are worrying about at the moment are not such a risk to the real economy as is being feared," he said.

articles.title_orig: Why Blizzard Made ‘World of Warcraft: Forever’
articles.title_zh: Why Blizzard Made ‘World of Warcraft: Forever’
articles.content_orig:
World of Warcraft Forever launched last night, and while there were a ton of people playing, the servers were remarkably stable . It turns out that Blizzard dedicated a ton of resources to making sure those servers were solid.
Last night, after the game launched, Blizzard tweeted out a meme from its World of Warcraft account, with a Gnome tapping a car with the WoW Forever logo, with a caption saying: "*Slaps Roof of WoW: Forever* This baby is running on: 3,924 Virtual Machines, 251,136 GB of Memory, 70,480 CPU Cores." That's a huge amount of memory, and it seems to have paid off with the smoothest Blizzard launch I've seen in years.
Blizzard's post bragging about the sheer amount of memory in its servers comes just a week after Sam Altman said in a podcast that it was "quite terrible" for people to have RAM in their own computers, rather than in a data center. Of course, he did later walk it back , instead claiming that he had "been arguing for the world to ramp up memory production for a long time." Still, that's 251,136GB of RAM that's dedicated to running an incredible MMO, rather than powering yet another AI data center.
*Slaps Roof of WoW: Forever* This baby is running on: 3,924 Virtual Machines 251,136 GB of Memory 70,480 CPU Cores https://t.co/P9PdRBzke7
Blizzard Executive Producer and Vice President for World of Warcraft Holly Longdale also posted celebrating the smooth launch, and said "this launch was crazier than the insanity we imagined but thankfully the team built plans and contingencies. They are incredible imo." And, while we likely will never know just how many people logged into Forever for the launch, I can say firsthand that there were hundreds of characters in the starting zone right at 6pm EST, so the team definitely deserves recognition for holding everything together.
Even on the WoW forums, which are hardly a bastion of positivity, there are a number of threads with players praising WoW Forever for being one of the smoothest WoW launches of all time . On X/Twitter, WoW streamer Darth Microtransaction posted, "I don’t know how they did it, but they did. World of Warcraft Forever launch was the smoothest launch I’ve seen. Almost 0 Que[ue]. 0 dc, and no lag."
This launch was a solid start to a game that's going to take most people weeks to go through. The beta was huge on its own, despite being limited to just level 30. And, even when folks knew their characters would get deleted, so many people played the beta that developers commented on it for being the "craziest numbers [they've] seen." And now that the full game is here, it's going to be interesting to see what players discover, and what gets added in the future. Because, according to Blizzard, there's potential to visit some fan favorite locations from future expansions , too.
Jackie Thomas is the Senior Tech Editor at IGN and the PC components queen. She's been covering gaming hardware for more than a decade for IGN, TechRadar, Gizmodo, PC Gamer and more. You can follow her @Jackiecobra

articles.title_orig: Where China Sees the Danger in a Wounded Trump
articles.title_zh: Where China Sees the Danger in a Wounded Trump
articles.content_orig:
China won’t be so quick to celebrate the stunning blue wave that washed over President Donald Trump this week.
American voters may have withdrawn the Republican mandate by giving Democrats the keys to Congress, but Trump can still direct his executive powers abroad, even as the opposition prepares to restrain him at home.
After a bruising midterm result for the U.S. president, a wounded Trump may seem like easy pickings for Chinese leader Xi Jinping , who will soon send negotiators to restart trade talks designed to neutralize America’s long-term tariff threat.
Xi had an understanding with Trump and knew what made him tick. But the political setback may make Trump much harder to predict .
Xi spent considerable resources on his rapprochement with Trump, including a state media campaign about Chinese resilience that stopped hostile economic acts by the United States and resulted in two glitzy state visits this year.
A promise to meet Trump at the APEC summit in southern China later this month, and again when Miami hosts the G20 meeting in December, has helped Xi build certainty into China’s relations with its top geopolitical rival.
Beijing may even go as far as to give Trump a foreign policy win at APEC by agreeing to a three-way meeting with Russia’s President Vladimir Putin in host city Shenzhen. Whether Xi makes any concrete commitments there is another question.
“Stability” has been the watchword in China for years, but it has extra weight this year after a campaign of purges swept up dozens of senior figures in elite Chinese politics and the military. Xi’s purges are about corruption in the Chinese Communist Party , but they’re also about loyalty—to him.
A recent gathering of the CCP’s Central Committee had the lowest attendance in over half a century, hinting at the scale of disciplinary action taken ahead of the party’s 21 st national congress in 12 months’ time, when Xi is widely expected to win an uncontested fourth 5-year term.
“Xi’s main political goal now is to secure another term at the 21st Party Congress. That requires not only a firm grip on power but also a case that his continued rule is legitimate and natural,” wrote Christopher Nye, a senior fellow at the Jamestown Foundation think tank.
Xi used the latest gathering of party cadres “to resolve the problems of legitimacy created by the purge,” Nye wrote this week.
A fourth term could extend Xi’s rule over China to 20 years.
So, 2027 will be a delicate year for Xi. He’ll be wary of a Trump unleashed , who, despite being weakened domestically, could channel his energy into foreign policy matters, namely negotiations with China to extend or rip up the Busan truce that kept tariffs at a minimum in exchange for Chinese agricultural purchases and other key commitments.
“Beijing could conclude the election results mean Trump needs an economic agreement more than China does…. In that sense, Beijing could turn Trump’s political setback into a bargaining miscalculation that unsettles the very stability Xi is trying to preserve,” said Craig Singleton, senior director of the China program at the Foundation for Defense of Democracies think tank.
“If Beijing expects last night’s result to humble Trump, it is probably mistaken. He may have less room politically at home, but that could produce even bolder executive action abroad, including new pressure on Chinese companies, tighter economic-security measures and faster reshoring.
"Beijing should be careful about mistaking Trump’s political weakness for restraint in his China policy ."
Trump’s first presidency also began with personal diplomacy with China’s Xi before flattery gave way to full-blown systemic confrontation.
Trump hosted Xi at Mar-a-Lago in spring 2017 and Xi returned the favor in fall with a lavish state visit for Trump in Beijing. The two leaders appeared to agree on $250 billion in commercial deals, which later never materialized.
The trade war followed in 2018, along with the first stage of the tech war that targeted Chinese telecoms giant Huawei the following year. The Phase One trade deal in early 2020 eased tensions but didn’t stop them from boiling over once more during the COVID-19 pandemic.
Beijing was so concerned by the downturn in relations and the mixed signals out of the White House that it feared an “ October surprise ,” a military strike to rally support before Trump’s presidential race with Democrat Joe Biden.
Gen. Mark Milley, then chairman of the Joint Chiefs of Staff, called his Chinese counterpart without Trump’s knowledge to assure him that the U.S. government was planning no such action—and to preempt any miscalculation by Beijing.
Trump’s last experience as a lame duck president didn’t lead to a hot war, but it locked in a new Cold War with China, one of economic decoupling and export controls. And on the last full day of the first Trump administration, his then secretary of state, Mike Pompeo, accused Xi’s government of genocide against Muslims in far-western China.
On the day Biden took office as the new U.S. president, China sanctioned former senior Trump officials in retaliation for the wild final weeks. The message to the new administration, and indeed the expectation, was that Trump’s hard-line China policies should be walked back. That didn’t happen and the rivalry was institutionalized.
Trump has no reason to hold back if Xi doesn’t play ball. And even with Trump neutered, the Democrats may not play nice.

articles.title_orig: Zelenskiy, Kyiv mayor trade blame as Russian strikes plunge city into darkness
articles.title_zh: Zelenskiy, Kyiv mayor trade blame as Russian strikes plunge city into darkness
articles.content_orig:
Yemen’s government forces and the Houthi rebel group are trading blame for an attack on the al-Hadara market in the Taiz governorate, that both sides say killed and injured dozens of people.
The spokesperson for the Yemeni government forces, Colonel Majed al-Nazili, said the “terrorist” Houthis struck the market on Friday with ballistic missiles, causing dozens of civilian casualties. He accused the Iran-backed group of committing a “war crime” and called for accountability.
The Houthis, however, accused Saudi Arabia, which backs Yemen’s internationally recognised government, of having launched three air strikes on the market, killing at least 30 civilians and injuring eight others.
Its Ministry of Health and Environment in the Yemeni Houthi-controlled capital Sanaa said Riyadh committed a “horrific crime” and called for an independent international investigation into Saudi Arabia’s “systematic targeting” of civilians.
Al Jazeera could not independently verify the reports,and there has been no response so far from the Saudi-led coalition forces.
Al Jazeera’s Yousef Mawry, reporting from Sanaa, said fighting has been ongoing in the al-Waziiya district where the market is located. The area is controlled by the Houthis, who are also known as Ansar Allah (Arabic for Supporters of God).
The Saudi-led coalition has been carrying out attacks on a daily basis to gain control of the district and its strategic mountain range, Mawry said.
“Whoever controls the al-Waziiya district controls the majority of the western Red Sea coastal line,” he added.
The Yemeni army said it recaptured several areas in the Taiz governorate on Friday, including the al-Nidani village, Shaab al-Sarari, large parts of the Sanamat area and the Ribat al-Qarn area in Dhi al-Barh.
Government forces also imposed a siege on entrances to the al-Sarari area, according to the military.
While the Houthis control much of the governorate, the city of Taiz is government-held. An ongoing Houthi siege on the city has lasted for 30 days and affected hundreds of thousands of people in the area.
The United Nations has repeatedly warned of a catastrophe inside Taiz city, where supplies of food and medicine are becoming increasingly scarce.
Yemen’s internationally recognised government launched Operation Dawn of Yemen on October 5  to take control of territories held by Houthi fighters.
Since the start of the military operation, neither Yemen’s government-controlled territories nor Saudi Arabia has been safe from Houthi missile attacks.
The Houthis have been firing missiles and drones daily into Saudi Arabia, hitting oil facilities and disrupting air traffic over the kingdom.

articles.title_orig: PSA: Want To Learn Link's Ocarina Tunes? Nintendo's Got The Sheet Music For All Of Them
articles.title_zh: PSA: Want To Learn Link's Ocarina Tunes? Nintendo's Got The Sheet Music For All Of Them
articles.content_orig:
Draw near, dear travelers, for you are about to hear a timeless tale. Of when a wise and kind princess escaped her castle in the cover of rain and night. When a powerful warrior unleashed his vile ambitions across an entire kingdom. And when a courageous hero fought back with a mastery over time itself…
That's right, all! The Legend of Zelda™: Ocarina of Time game is out now, exclusively for the Nintendo Switch™ 2 system! On his quest to stop the evil Ganondorf, Link (and his fairy companion, Navi) will explore the kingdom of Hyrule, venture into dungeons to acquire weapons, and use their combined smarts to solve tricky puzzles.
(Oh, and did we mention that you'll be doing this across two different time periods using time-travel powers? Why yes, you will!)
Don't worry if you've never played a Legend of Zelda game before or have only played the most recent ones—this is a great jumping off point to learn what the series is all about.
The original tale first debuted on the Nintendo 64™ system way back in 1998 and…a lot has changed since then.
This new version of the game has completely overhauled visuals, voiced cutscenes, expanded dialogue, symphonic orchestral music, reworked camera and movement controls, and more. You can challenge powerful enemies again in the Hall of Fallen Foes, and search for fairy thoughts scattered across Hyrule to learn fun little tidbits. Please check out the trailers below to get a better idea of what the game looks like in motion.
The Legend of Zelda: Ocarina of Time is a standalone adventure, and it's also a great intro to what the series is all about—a combo of action, exploration, puzzle solving, epic storylines, memorable characters/music, and…treasure chest opening. You'll climb to the volcanic tops of Death Mountain and dive to the watery depths of Zora Domain. You'll meet mysterious warriors like Sheik and Impa and learn of the Triforce. It's a classic fight between good and evil.
Music plays a big role, too. You'll use Link's ocarina to manipulate the world around you—from changing night into day to calling your trusty steed, Epona. If you're feeling extra musical, the built-in microphone on your system also lets you play the in-game ocarina by humming or playing your own instrument.
And of course, you'll also be playing as both young Link and adult Link in two separate time periods. How does Hyrule change between the two periods? Well…that would be a spoiler…
Get more out of your adventure with ZELDA NOTES —a game-specific service found in the Nintendo Switch App* for smart devices. With ZELDA NOTES, you can:
See your accomplishments for the day
Challenge yourself to find in-game locations based on in-app images (and then exchange the points you get for music scores that can be played on the in-app ocarina)
Make your own music scores and share via QR code
Take the Ocarina of Time Quiz to test your game knowledge
And for you digital card collectors out there, you may want to check out the free Nintendo Today! app** for mobile devices. Currently, you can collect cards in the app that are inspired by different Legend of Zelda games.
2026 marks the 40th anniversary of the Legend of Zelda series, and we wanted to take a moment to thank all the fans who bring their passion and love to the series. You're the ones who make it special, and we hope you continue to enjoy Link and Zelda's adventures!

articles.title_orig: Taiwan to close representative office in Papua New Guinea, blames China
articles.title_zh: Taiwan to close representative office in Papua New Guinea, blames China
articles.content_orig:
Taiwan says it is closing its representative office in Papua New Guinea and will stop buying liquefied natural gas (LNG) from the country, blaming Chinese political pressure on the South Pacific nation.
Taiwan’s Ministry of Foreign Affairs said on Friday that Papua New Guinea had repeated previous demands that staff leave its office in the capital, Port Moresby, within a set deadline and had pushed for ⁠its closure.
These actions “reflect China’s continued use of political pressure and economic influence to interfere in other countries’ diplomatic decisions and suppress Taiwan’s international space”, it said in a statement.
China, which claims Taiwan as part of its territory, had welcomed Papua New Guinea’s decision in July to shutter Taiwan’s office in Port Moresby. Taipei rejected the move, and the office remained open in the interim.
The Pacific has long been an area for diplomatic competition between China and Taiwan. Papua New Guinea has formal diplomatic relations with China, but it had allowed Taiwan to have a representative office in Port Moresby.
Taiwan has formal diplomatic ties with only three Pacific Islands nations: Palau, Tuvalu and the Marshall Islands. It also has a representative office in Fiji. Just 12 countries maintain formal ⁠diplomatic ties with Taiwan.
Taiwan previously announced that it had stopped spot purchases of LNG from the South Pacific nation, but on Friday the ministry said it also would no longer sign new spot purchase contracts with the country.
Taiwanese LNG purchases accounted for one-third of Papua New Guinea’s exports.
Last year, Taiwan imported about 8 percent of its natural gas from Port Moresby.
Taipei will also end technical cooperation and assistance programmes, “including medical missions, related scholarship and talent development programmes”, the ministry said.

articles.title_orig: 3 foreign nationals allegedly used AI to mimic CEOs in $129M scheme, DOJ says
articles.title_zh: 3 foreign nationals allegedly used AI to mimic CEOs in $129M scheme, DOJ says
articles.content_orig:
Three foreign nationals have been charged in connection with an alleged international fraud scheme that federal prosecutors say used AI technology to impersonate corporate executives and attorneys and steal more than $129 million.
According to an indictment filed in the Southern District of New York , Jacob Soall, who went by “Rocky Balboa” and “Seba Clarke,” was arrested in Spain in June; Sharon Hazan, who used the nicknames “Superman Cash,” “Impossible Mission,” “Fat Boy” and “Ron,” was arrested in Spain in August; and Guy Sheetrit was arrested in the United Kingdom in September.
All three are accused of participating in a scheme that ran from July 2024 to February 2026 involving the use of artificial intelligence to impersonate the voices and images of corporate executives and attorneys at major law firms to trick employees of several companies into transferring large sums of money to bank accounts controlled by the group, according to a press release from the U.S. attorney’s office.
The trio and their co-conspirators would tell these employees — typically in accounting departments — they needed help with a confidential financial transaction and would use AI technology to mimic the company CEO’s voice, according to the press release.
Then, while pretending to be the CEO, they would tell employees to contact attorneys at large international law firms who they said were also working on the transactions, but in reality, those “attorneys” were also part of the scheme, prosecutors said.
Finally, one of the people involved in the scheme would instruct the employee to wire large amounts of money to bank accounts set up worldwide, according to the press release.
Once the employee wired the money, the group would convert the cash into cryptocurrency “in an attempt to conceal the source, ownership, and control of the stolen proceeds and distribute it amongst themselves and their co-conspirators,” prosecutors said.
The U.S. attorney’s office alleges the scheme stole more than $129 million from companies worldwide, including an investment bank in New York, a hospital system in Missouri, a bank in Rhode Island, a hospital system in California, a financial technology company in the U.K., a mutual fund company in Massachusetts and a pet food company in Florida.
Soall, from Spain and the U.K., impersonated U.K. attorneys and used a script titled “Lawyer Call” to make himself seem like a real attorney when speaking with victims, the release said.
Hazan, from Israel, laundered the money from the scheme, according to the press release. Prosecutors allege that Hazan “boasted that he had been laundering money since 1994; that he had laundered over $400 million in just the past three years; and that, among professional money launderers, he was ‘number one all over the world.’”
Hazan was also convicted of conspiracy to commit bank fraud in the Southern District of New York in 2008.
Sheetrit, from Israel and the United Arab Emirates, is also accused of laundering funds, the press release said.
All three have been charged with conspiracy to commit wire fraud, wire fraud, two counts of aggravated identity theft, money laundering conspiracy and two counts of money laundering. Each of the seven charges carries a maximum prison sentence of 20 years.
“SI technology offers tremendous potential. But the public should recognize that there are some who seek to use this emerging technology to pursue criminal goals,” U.S. Attorney Jamie McDonald said in the release, using an abbreviation for super intelligence, the White House’s preferred term for artificial intelligence. “I encourage individuals and the business community to consider how to best protect themselves from the emerging threat of SI-enabled crime.”
Rebecca Cohen is a breaking news reporter for NBC News Digital.

articles.title_orig: Denmark’s top court to rule on ‘parallel societies’ after ‘non-western’ people evicted
articles.title_zh: Denmark’s top court to rule on ‘parallel societies’ after ‘non-western’ people evicted
articles.content_orig:
Seven families from Helsingor, a coastal city north of Copenhagen, are facing their former landlord in Denmark’s Supreme Court.
In a two-day hearing that began on Friday, they are arguing they were forced from their homes because of where they, or their parents, come from.
Their leases were terminated in 2022 under a 2018 law, once known as the “ ghetto law ”, which targets social housing estates where more than half of residents are classed as “non-Western”. The government claims the law is aimed at integration. But rights groups have for years fought against the measures, saying they are discriminatory.
“It’s about whether the criteria regarding the tenants’ origin is neutral or not,” Eddie Khawaja, the families’ lawyer, told the news agency AFP.
So what does “non-Western” mean, and could the courts bring the law down? Here’s what you need to know:
It is a statistical label that covers most of the world.
In 2020, the UN Human Rights Office said: “Statistics Denmark, under the Danish Ministry for Economic and Interior Affairs, defines ‘non-Western’ as any country outside the EU, with the exceptions of Andorra, Australia, Canada, Iceland, Liechtenstein, Monaco, New Zealand, Norway, San Marino, Switzerland, the USA, and the Vatican State.
“The effect is that ‘non-Western’ disproportionately means Denmark’s non-white, non-European ethnic populations,” it stated. The label also covers descendants: anyone born in Denmark if neither parent is a Danish citizen born in the country.
That means a Danish citizen born and raised in Copenhagen can still be “non-Western”.
Every December 1, the government names “parallel societies”.
These are social housing areas of at least 1,000 people where more than 50 percent are “non-Western” immigrants and descendants.
An area must also meet two of four criteria on unemployment, crime, education, and income.
Areas on the list for five years become “transformation areas”, which the government used to call “hard ghettos”.
They must cut public family housing to 40 percent by 2030 through sales, demolition or conversion.
An estate with the same social problems but fewer “non-Western” residents faces no such obligation.
The government says the goal is integration.
The law was part of a plan called “One Denmark without Parallel Societies: No Ghettos in 2030”.
In 2021, Kaare Dybvad Bek, then interior minister, said too many non-Western foreigners in one area “increases the risk of an emergence of religious and cultural parallel societies”.
About 11,000 people across Denmark will have to leave their homes by 2030, according to tenants’ associations.
In Helsingor, the landlord Boliggarden announced in early 2020 that it would renovate 96 apartments at the Nojsomhed estate. It then terminated the tenants’ leases. Most of those tenants were of foreign origin.
“They didn’t want the estate to be labelled ‘hard ghetto’ so they wanted to forcibly move us out when we advocated for other solutions,” Riad, a 33-year-old plaintiff who did not want his family name published, told AFP.
The law may be discriminatory, but Danish judges ultimately make the final decision about whether it violated Danish laws prohibiting ethnic discrimination.
The Court of Justice of the European Union (CJEU) ruled in December 2025, in cases brought by tenants from Mjolnerparken in Copenhagen and Schackenborgvaenge in Slagelse. It said nationality or country of birth alone does not determine ethnic origin, but an allegedly neutral criterion covering many origins could be linked to ethnicity.
That runs contrary to the Danish government’s position and the reasoning of the lower Danish courts in the Helsingor case, which found that the “non-Western” does not describe an ethnic group and therefore did not result in discrimination that violated Denmark’s Equal Treatment Act.
Danish judges must decide whether the “non-Western” criterion really rests on residents’ ethnic origin, the court said, and consequently, if people included in the criterion are afforded less favourable treatment.
Less favourable treatment, it noted, could include “an increased risk of early termination of their leases”.
In January, Sophie Haestorp Andersen, then minister for social affairs and housing, told a parliamentary hearing that authorities must keep applying the law until the Eastern High Court rules, the Danish outlet Danske Kommuner reported.
The four-party coalition in power since June includes the Green Left (SF), which voted for the law in 2018, according to the public broadcaster DR. The party’s Jacob Mark is now minister for children, elderly affairs and housing.
No date has been officially set for the verdict, but reports suggest it could be handed down later this month.
If the families win, they would probably be rehoused in homes similar to the ones they had to leave.
The Mjolnerparken case is still before the Eastern High Court.

articles.title_orig: OpenAI will keep investing in AI data centers despite election results, CFO tells CNBC
articles.title_zh: OpenAI will keep investing in AI data centers despite election results, CFO tells CNBC
articles.content_orig:
OpenAI CFO Sarah Friar on Friday said the company will continue to invest in artificial intelligence infrastructure, even after voters strongly opposed data centers during Tuesday's midterm elections.
"When I think about the midterms, I need to keep thinking about how do we keep investing to meet that customer demand," Friar told CNBC's Sara Eisen in an interview at the Citi TMT Leadership Summit in Pebble Beach, California. "It starts early with having built relationships with all of the hyperscalers, and it will continue to mean that we raise capital."
Out of 41 local ballot measures across 10 states, voters backed restrictions or rejected pro-development measures in all but one, according to an analysis by Ballotpedia and additional results gathered by CNBC on Wednesday. Opposition to the facilities mounted swiftly over the summer as Americans grew worried about their potential to harm the environment, raise utility bills and contribute to job loss.
Investors have turned skeptical on the AI trade of late due to a combination of higher borrowing costs, concerns about soaring debt and public backlash toward the industry. The Nasdaq on Thursday suffered its steepest drop in 19 months, led by a plunge in shares of the chipmakers and neocloud companies most closely tied to the AI buildout. The stocks rebounded some on Friday.
OpenAI depends on data centers to train its AI models and serve customers, and Friar said she doesn't think the election results dramatically changed anything for the company. On Thursday, OpenAI published a policy blueprint and a series of commitments that it pledged to apply to company-owned and -operated data centers in the future.
"If the midterm means more focus on data centers and communities, we're going to keep doing the work to get into those communities and to build trust with them," Friar said.
OpenAI confidentially filed its prospectus with the Securities and Exchange Commission in June, and Friar said Friday that the company would continue to look into a 2027 debut. Anthropic, OpenAI's chief rival, is trying to go public first, with an aim to hit the Nasdaq in mid-November.
Anthropic's revenue in the first nine months of the year jumped roughly 1,200% to $33.2 billion, according to its prospectus. The company said it has entered into purchase commitments and lease agreements with an aggregate committed spend of about $895.4 billion, "substantially all of which is related to compute and infrastructure."
OpenAI is in talks to raise funding at a $1.25 billion pre-money valuation, Friar said Friday. She said "a good CFO always raises money when she can" and that the round is ongoing.
"The demand for AI is real," Friar said. "I don't think anyone's arguing with that, or if they are, I think it's a losing argument."

articles.title_orig: NYC schools’ standoff with Google over AI raises prospect of no search in class
articles.title_zh: NYC schools’ standoff with Google over AI raises prospect of no search in class
articles.content_orig:
Sen. Bernie Sanders and New York City Mayor Zohran Mamdani criticized the policy, which Google says gives schools more control
Google $GOOGL will cut off Google Search for schools that opt out of its AI tools, according to CNN .
Google announced changes to school controls on Tuesday that switch off Gemini, Gemini Notebook, Gemini in Classroom and Google Search on accounts for K-12 students until a school's administrators enable them. The company said it will give schools more detail over the next several months, before the rollout begins.
Chris Phillips, Google 's vice president for education, said schools that ban AI "will not have access to search, and they'll see a message from their school that indicates it's not available," according to CNN. Phillips said "Search and AI are deeply integrated," according to TechCrunch .
Google responded on X $TWTR that the changes give schools "more choice, not less," and that each of Gemini, Gemini Notebook and Search can be enabled by a school separately from the others, according to CNN. The same post says AI Mode and AI Overview will walk students through problems one step at a time. That suggests schools would have no way to run Search while avoiding its AI features.
Google also said it will pilot Guided Learning in Search for student accounts at select U.S. schools later this month. The feature is meant to walk students through homework problems instead of giving direct answers.
Criticism came from several political figures, according to TechCrunch. Sen. Bernie Sanders (I-VT) accused Google of "extortion," and Sen. Richard Blumenthal (D-CT) said Google is "more concerned with forcing Gemini into schools than enabling students to succeed." Lina Khan, the former Federal Trade Commission chair, called the move anticompetitive.
New York City Mayor Zohran Mamdani wrote on X that "No corporation should have the power to dictate how we teach our children," according to CNN.
New York City schools spokesperson Nicole Brownstein said officials are "reaching out to Google to discuss this update further," according to Gothamist . She said Gemini and AI Mode are now turned off on the Chromebooks given to city students, and the city has asked Google to remove AI Overview from search results.
Google 's move follows pushback over AI in schools . In August, Google turned on its Gemini chatbot by default in Classroom for schools that allow student use, a decision school leaders criticized. In early September, New York City banned generative AI for students through eighth grade for the current school year, and Los Angeles Unified turned it off on district-issued devices.
Blumenthal and Sen. Josh Hawley sent a letter to Google CEO Sundar Pichai asking what the company knows about how its AI products affect children's mental health and learning. They set a Nov. 2 deadline for a reply.

articles.title_orig: UN climate talks start in the year of disasters, energy price shocks and fast rising temperatures
articles.title_zh: UN climate talks start in the year of disasters, energy price shocks and fast rising temperatures
articles.content_orig:
The move to clean electricity will form the focus of the climate summit, which begins next week in coal-obsessed Turkey. The outlook doesn’t look good
Don’t get Down to Earth delivered to your inbox? Sign up here
H olding a climate conference under the presidency of one coal-obsessed country might be regarded as a misfortune for the planet – sharing it between two starts to look provocative. But at this year’s Cop31 UN climate summit in Antalya, coal exporter Australia and coal consumer Turkey will be trying to shift the focus away from dirty fossil fuels and towards clean electricity, with a target on the table to meet 35% of final energy demand from electricity by 2035.
Will they succeed? The geopolitical outlook for Cop31 is worse than for almost any recent “conference of the parties” under the UN Framework Convention on Climate Change (UNFCCC). Conflicts in Ukraine, Iran and Gaza are destabilising global alliances, an unpredictable White House is sowing economic uncertainty and AI is threatening to unleash digitised chaos.
But with an El Niño weather system supercharged by fossil fuels already wreaking havoc and yet to peak, the climate is showing where the real potential for earthbound catastrophe lies. For the next fortnight, Down to Earth will bring you twice-weekly updates from the Cop31 negotiations plus, when the gavel finally comes down, a final assessment of what progress has been made – and where negotiations have fallen short in Antalya.
But first, this week’s most important reads.
‘Bunch of baloney’: calls grow for Cop summit reforms as countries on track to fail nature targets
The Amazon’s canary in the coalmine: what a tropical fish can tell us about climate upheaval
The next global pandemic could be brewing on a mink farm in Utah – and little is being done to stop it
That Cop31 is happening in Antalya, but presided over by Australia, is the product of a last-minute compromise struck last year at Cop30 in Belém. Australia had wanted to hold a Cop since 2021, when Anthony Albanese made it one of his key promises ahead of the climate-inflected general election he won the next year. Turkey has also wanted to hold a Cop for some time, and claimed to have agreed with the UK, hosts of the Glasgow Cop26 conference in 2021 , that 2026 would be its year.
For complicated reasons dating back to 1992, when the UNFCCC was signed, Australia and Turkey fall in the same group as western Europe when it comes to being allowed to bid for the presidency, which rotates annually between five regional groups. There is no mechanism within the treaty for resolving situations where two countries cannot agree on their bid, and no provision for a majority vote to decide among competing options.
Despite this inauspicious start, the two countries seem to have worked well together in the run-up. Australia will chair the negotiations, taking charge of issues such as the “just transition” to help workers in fossil fuels adjust to a low-carbon economy, the loss and damage fund (which has come into renewed focus after the catastrophic glacier collapse in Nepal ), other forms of climate finance and progress on emissions cuts.
Turkey will take charge of the “action agenda”, which is a programme of voluntary commitments that runs alongside the formal negotiations. This year, the quest to electrify the global economy will be the central plank, with initiatives on cutting waste and methane – two topics beloved of Turkey’s first lady, Emine Erdoğan – also on the list.
Cop31 is also the first major international meeting after several momentous elections: the US midterms, which delivered a pummelling to Donald Trump and the Republicans, and Brazil’s presidential poll, won by the president, Lula da Silva. The latter was regarded as a relief for the Amazon , which Lula’s opponent, Flávio Bolsonaro, was likely to have opened up to further rampant exploitation.
And it is the last such outing for another familiar figure – António Guterres, who has used his two terms as secretary-general of the UN to speak out on the climate as none other . Expect a fiery farewell.
With some items of good news to celebrate, the outlook for Cop31 is not all bleak. But delegates would do well to read the latest UN reports on what it will take to minimise the now inevitable overshoot of the 1.5C threshold. Preventing temperatures rising beyond 1.8C will require massive and urgent cuts to greenhouse gas emissions, while global carbon emissions have yet to peak. Phasing out fossil fuels has never been so urgent.
after newsletter promotion
Inevitably, the fossil fuel predilections of both hosts will come under scrutiny. Australia could start to shift its reliance on fossil fuel exports in favour of clean electricity, Australia’s Cop31 president of negotiations, Chris Bowen, told the Guardian when we caught up with him at the mid-year climate talks in Bonn in June. But he refused to put any kind of end date on coal.
Coal remains Turkey’s biggest source of power, despite a push for renewable energy, and the country’s national climate plan allows for an increase in its greenhouse gas emissions, rather than a cut. A group of 50 frontline organisations from Turkey, Australia and other coal regions around the world wrote to the Cop presidents this week to call for an end to coal mining and use.
Mehmet Dalkanat from the Afşin-Elbistan Platform for the Protection of Life and Nature in Turkey said: “People in Afşin-Elbistan have lived with coal for 40 years and have already paid a heavy price in pollution and the impacts of coal.” He points towards the cancellation of plans to expand the country’s largest coal-fired power plant in July. “[This was] a major victory for local communities who have been fighting for years, and a powerful source of hope for a coal-free future,” he said. “The Cop31 presidencies must build on this local victory to accelerate the phaseout of coal and deliver a just transition.”
Though freedom of expression is curtailed in Turkey – as it has been in three of the previous four Cop host countries – expect more such protests in Antalya. We’ll be following developments throughout the summit, with our daily liveblog bringing you news, analysis – and a look behind the scenes of one of the most vital meetings on the planet.

articles.title_orig: Russia using own version of Starlink for military comms over Ukraine, Kyiv says
articles.title_zh: Russia using own version of Starlink for military comms over Ukraine, Kyiv says
articles.content_orig:
Russia is building its own satellite network to expand its military capabilities. RASSVET system could eventually allow Russian forces to control attack drones over much greater distances, threatening countries beyond Ukraine. With Belarus helping develop the network’s ground infrastructure, the Baltic states could face a new security threat on NATO’s eastern flank.
RASSVET is a low Earth orbit satellite communications network that has been under development since 2023 by the private Russian company Bureau 1440, with state support.
In 2026, funding and deployment of the project accelerated after Russia lost access to Starlink , dealing a significant blow to its offensive capabilities. RASSVET aims to replicate the American system and establish Russia’s own independent satellite internet network.
Its successful deployment would pose a threat not only to Ukraine but also to Russia’s neighbors, particularly the Baltic states.
To make the system fully operational, Moscow is involving its allies, particularly Belarus. A ground control facility is being built there, providing the infrastructure needed to expand the system’s coverage. The project’s local partner is Belintersat, a Belarusian satellite operator.
For now, Ukraine faces the most immediate threat from RASSVET’s deployment. However, the construction of the necessary infrastructure in Belarus is already expanding the system’s geographical reach. RASSVET could also pose a threat to the Baltic states—Lithuania, Latvia, and Estonia—which are located near Russia and Belarus.
The potential threat is substantial. Thousands of Russian drones could carry out precision strikes against military facilities and critical infrastructure in countries that may not be prepared to repel such an attack. Most importantly, these strikes could be carried out with relatively inexpensive drones, while defending against them would be costly. This challenge has already become evident during the war in the Middle East.
While RASSVET has yet to reach its planned operational capacity , its potential military applications are already becoming apparent in Ukraine.
In Russia, RASSVET is primarily presented as a civilian project, but the reality tells a different story.
Ukrainian military personnel have already documented the use of the system’s terminals on Molniya drones —inexpensive fixed-wing attack drones capable of traveling dozens of kilometers.
For now, Ukraine faces the most immediate threat from RASSVET’s deployment. Equipped with satellite terminals, Russian drones would be able to carry out more precise strikes deep inside Ukrainian territory. Countering such attacks would become more difficult because the drones would be controlled through a satellite communications network.
Notably, although the system is being deployed gradually, it is already being used on the battlefield. Between 2023 and 2024, the first six test satellites were launched into orbit. In 2026, following the suspension of Starlink services, development accelerated, with dozens of satellites launched into orbit. Although not all of them reached their designated orbital positions or became operational, the project is moving forward.
The Kremlin plans to have 250 satellites in orbit by 2027, 730 by 2030, and more than 900 by 2035.
Russia is well aware of the capabilities of its new satellite system and is already waging a hybrid war against its main competitor, Starlink. Over the past month, SpaceX infrastructure has been attacked three times in European countries . Infrastructure essential to Starlink’s operations was damaged in Poland, Bulgaria, and Lithuania.
In October, Axios also reported that a Russian satellite had approached the American ICEYE-X36 satellite to within just a few dozen meters. This could have been an attempt to interfere with American satellite equipment. Russia may be testing potential methods of interference while also gauging how other countries might respond.
One way to counter this threat is through sanctions. As of now, Belintersat is subject to sanctions imposed by all major jurisdictions, including the United States and the European Union. The problem, however, is that only the United States has imposed sanctions on the Russian company Bureau 1440.
European countries are also exploring technological countermeasures. Germany is assessing ground-based systems capable of disrupting satellite communications and navigation signals, potentially enabling interference with RASSVET’s operations.
Ukraine, meanwhile, is pushing for international restrictions on the Russian satellite network. Moscow has included Ukrainian territory in the declared service areas of its RASSVET-1 and RASSVET-3 systems, prompting Kyiv to appeal to the International Telecommunication Union (ITU).
Ukraine is demanding that its territory be excluded from the networks’ declared service areas and has raised concerns about potential interference with Ukrainian communications systems. Kyiv is also urging other countries whose territories Russia has included in its planned coverage areas to submit similar objections.
Another approach is, at the very least, to prepare for countermeasures. Starlink currently does not operate in Russia, and SpaceX prohibits such use of its services. However, allowing Starlink to operate even a few hundred kilometers into Russian territory could potentially expand Ukraine’s ability to conduct drone operations against Russian military equipment farther from the border, including ballistic missile launchers. This could help reduce threats to border regions in Ukraine and neighboring countries.

articles.content_orig:
Odds that Anthropic will announce a public offering fell in recent days on Kalshi as AI-related stocks slid after Democrats won control of Congress and several key governorships.
In the last week, odds that Anthropic would announce an IPO before December fell to 57% from over 85% on Kalshi. Chances that the company would announce a public offering before January also dropped to 68% from 90% in the last week. The contract asks when Anthropic will officially announce an IPO and will be verified by news outlets.
The AI company confidentially filed its IPO prospectus with the Securities and Exchange Commission back in June.
The repricing on Kalshi came as investors grew concerned that Democratic victories across both chambers could slow data center construction, making the bet on AI less attractive.
Gov.-elect Gina Hinojosa of Texas, a Democrat who ousted three-term Republican Greg Abbott, championed tighter protocols against data center buildout in her state during her campaign.
"We will have laws to protect Texans and we need to stop what we are doing with data centers until we have those protections," the Democrat told CNN on Thursday.
The Nasdaq Composite closed Thursday more than 10% below its most recent high, crossing the benchmark for what Wall Street views as a correction. The S&P 500 lost 4.4%, while the Dow Jones Industrial Average fell more than 1,800 points, or 3.4%. Stocks were attempting to rebound on Friday, with the Nasdaq gaining 1.3% and the S&P 500 rising 0.7%. The Dow shed 0.2%.
On Friday, shares of Micron Technology and Nvidia each gained about 4%, after falling 17% and 9%, respectively, the day before. CoreWeave shares also rose more than 2% Friday morning after tumbling about 10% on Wednesday. Even if Friday's gains are sustained, these stocks have tallied steep losses over the past week.

articles.title_orig: US economy adds 165,000 jobs in October, blowing past expectations
articles.title_zh: US economy adds 165,000 jobs in October, blowing past expectations
articles.content_orig:
Kenny Polcari discusses the historical S&P 500 performance following midterm elections. He predicts the stock market will be higher in 12 months, continuing a trend seen in every midterm cycle since World War II.
The U.S. economy added jobs at a strong pace in October, rebounding from a softer September amid economic uncertainty.
The Bureau of Labor Statistics on Friday reported that employers added 165,000 jobs in October. That figure was well above the 65,000 estimate of economists polled by LSEG.
The unemployment rate decreased slightly to 4.1%, which was lower than the expectations of economists who predicted it would hold steady at 4.2%.
Revisions were made to the payroll numbers for the prior two months, with August revised up by 53,000 from a gain of 133,000 jobs to 186,000 jobs; while the change for September was revised up by 31,000 jobs from a gain of 29,000 to 60,000.
Taken together, employment in August and September was 84,000 higher than previously reported.
TRUMP ADMIN NAMES NEW ECONOMIC OPPORTUNITY ZONES TO SPUR PRIVATE INVESTMENT IN STRUGGLING COMMUNITIES
Private payrolls grew by 159,000 jobs in October, well above the 64,000 expected by economists polled by LSEG.
Government payrolls increased by 6,000 jobs in October. The sector's loss of 17,000 jobs in September was revised down to a loss of 18,000 jobs. The federal government shed 1,000 jobs in October, while state governments added 8,000 jobs and local governments cut 1,000 roles last month.
The manufacturing sector added 19,000 jobs in October, well above the gain of 5,000 that was predicted by economists polled by LSEG. September's gain of 9,000 jobs was also revised up to 13,000. Professional and business services added 70,000 jobs in October, which was well above the average monthly gain of 15,000 jobs over the past 12 months. The sector's job growth was led by gains in professional, scientific and technical services (+32,900), and in administrative and support and waste management and remediation services (+28,100).
Healthcare added 41,600 jobs in October, above the average monthly gain of 31,000 over the last 12 months. Most of last month's gains were in hospitals (+16,000), home healthcare services (+10,500) and outpatient care centers (+4,800).
Transportation and warehousing added 24,800 jobs last month, with growth occurring among couriers and messengers (+17,400) and air transportation (+3,500).
Private payrolls grew by 159,000 in October, well above the expectations of a gain of 64,000 jobs. (Al Drago/Bloomberg via Getty Images)
PRIVATE SECTOR ADDED 86,000 JOBS IN OCTOBER, ABOVE EXPECTATIONS, ADP SAYS
The number of long-term unemployed, defined as those who have been jobless for 27 weeks or more, was 2 million in October and changed little over the month. The long-term unemployed accounted for 27.6% of all unemployed people.
The number of people employed part-time for economic reasons rose by 339,000 to 4.8 million in October. These individuals would've preferred full-time work but were working part-time because their hours were reduced, or they were unable to find full-time jobs.
The labor force participation was 61.9% in October, while the employment-population ratio was 59.3%. Both of these figures were little changed in October and have shown little net change since January.
Average hourly earnings increased 3.1% year over year in October, above the 2.4% rise predicted by LSEG economists. Earnings also grew 0.4% on a monthly basis, above the 0.3% estimate in the LSEG poll.
FED'S PREFERRED INFLATION GAUGE ROSE IN SEPTEMBER AS THIRD-QUARTER GDP BEATS EXPECTATIONS
Federal Reserve Chair Kevin Warsh and central bank policymakers will hold their next interest rate meeting on December 8-9. (Daniel Heuer/Bloomberg via Getty Images)
Seema Shah, chief global strategist at Principal Asset Management, said in a statement that the October jobs report "is a strong rebuttal to fears that the economy is heading into a meaningful slowdown."
"Payrolls growth surprised firmly to the upside, unemployment fell back to 4.1%, and job creation remains broad-based, pointing to an economy that is still absorbing labor comfortably rather than one beginning to buckle under tighter financial conditions," Shah said. "With wage growth also picking up, a December Fed hike remains firmly on the table despite the recent tightening in financial conditions."
Lindsay Rosner, head of multi-sector fixed income investing at Goldman Sachs Asset Management, said that the October jobs report's "payroll number removed the traffic light at the December intersection for the Fed."
"Fed focus was already firmly on moderating inflation , and continued signs of tightening in the labor market give it a license to raise rates without hindering its employment mandate. Additional tightening is possible in the first quarter if inflation continues to print strong," Rosner added.
The strong October jobs report raised the likelihood of the Federal Reserve hiking interest rates when it holds its next meeting on Dec. 8-9.
The market's expectations of a 25-basis-point rate hike ticked up on Friday, with the CME FedWatch tool showing a 76.8% probability the Fed hikes in December – an increase from 66.9% a week ago. A hike of that size would take the federal funds rate to a target range of 4% to 4.25%.

The benchmark S&P 500 Index rose 0.65% during Friday morning's trading session.
The Dow Jones Industrial Average slipped 0.2%, while the Nasdaq Composite rose 1.25%.

articles.title_orig: Nasdaq rebounds as chip stocks recover from steep losses
articles.title_zh: Nasdaq rebounds as chip stocks recover from steep losses
articles.content_orig:
Asian and European markets follow US tech rout with many analysts predicting more waves of selling to come
European and Asian stock markets fell sharply on Friday after the Democrats’ decisive victory in the midterms triggered a rout in US tech stocks a day earlier.
A sell-off on Wall Street on Thursday was followed by sharp falls in Asian stock markets on Friday. The investor sentiment then reached London, where the market was, at one stage, poised for its worst day since March.
The FTSE 100 index, which tracks blue-chip shares listed in London, was down as much as 254 points, or 2.35%, at 10,528 points during a wave of selling in morning trading. But by the close of the day it had clawed back some of its losses to be down 1%, helped by a rise in US stocks when Wall Street reopened.
Germany’s Dax index fell by 2%, France’s Cac 40 dropped by 0.8% and Spain’s Ibex lost 0.6%.
Susannah Streeter, the chief investment strategist at Wealth Club, said: “The tech sell-off has intensified, with the pain of the brutal sell-off on Wall Street carried straight through to Asia and knocking sentiment in Europe .
“Big worries are colliding – the build-out of datacentres looks set to slow, which risks shredding the spending spree underpinning the boom, right at the time that investors have become super nervous about returns on this massive investment.”
However, there were signs of easing jitters on Wall Street on Friday, where tech stocks rose in early trading, lifting the S&P 500 share index by 0.8% by early afternoon in New York and the Nasdaq by 1.6% – which only recovered a portion of their previous day’s losses.
That followed a stronger-than-expected employment report that showed the US economy added 165,000 new jobs in October, pulling the unemployment rate down to 4.1%.
On Thursday, the Nasdaq share index had its worst day in 19 months after slumping 5.5%.
Chip stocks led the slump on Thursday, with the memory maker SanDisk tumbling by 22% and the hard drive maker Western Digital falling by 17%. Wall Street’s “fear index”, the Vix, jumped by more than 60% to its highest levels since the early weeks of the Iran war, in a sign of rising market volatility.
The heavy falls continued in Asia on Friday, with Japan’s Nikkei 225 index sinking 6% and South Korea’s Kospi index tumbling more than 6.5%.
“It’s actually a bit of a disaster,” said Christopher Forbes, the head of Asia and Middle East at CMC Markets.
“[Clients] were long index, long stocks, and they all got carried out. All night, all day – we had client margin calls, client complaints … because it’s a very emotional thing, right? People are wedded to their positions and views on a stock or outcome, and you’re telling them: ‘Look, you’ve just lost money.’”
Chris Beauchamp, the chief market analyst at the investing and trading platform IG, said: “Yesterday’s [Thursday’s] brutal session marked a dramatic turnaround from Wednesday, but with AI fears still prominent there is a risk that there is much more selling to come.
after newsletter promotion
“Investors remain on watch for a potential resumption of the Iran conflict, and are nervously watching the oil price after its slump earlier in the week. All in all it remains a very febrile atmosphere.”
However, despite the sharp losses suffered on global stock markets around the world, most indices are still up for the year. The Nasdaq Composite index remains up 6.35% since the start of January – even though it is more than 10% below its peak.
The FTSE 100 has gained almost 7.5% in 2026 – but it is now more than 300 points below the record high set in July.
Mohit Kumar, an economist at the investment bank Jefferies, said that while he did not expect a quick rebound from Thursday’s losses in the US, he also did not believe it marked the “start of the unwind of the AI trade”.
He said: “AI investment has been a key driver of US growth and we do not see the Democrats as giving up on this growth engine. Datacentres and AI infrastructure also create jobs and Democrats would be reluctant to let those jobs move on to other states or outside the country.”
Stock market tremors have also hit the London Metal Exchange, with copper poised for its biggest weekly fall since March.
Benchmark three-month copper, a key metal used in the semiconductor, electronics and automotive industry, has dropped 0.61%, leaving it positioned for a 2.79% fall this week.
Craig Lang, a principal analyst at the consultancy CRU, said the price of copper was increasingly influenced by the AI market and “sentiment towards datacentre expansion”.

articles.title_orig: Europe alarmed by US plans for security deal with Russia
articles.title_zh: Europe alarmed by US plans for security deal with Russia
articles.content_orig:
BRUSSELS — Europe is once again watching the White House through gritted teeth.
An opaque Trump administration proposal for a new European-wide security arrangement with Russia has met skepticism from European capitals that fear it risks sidelining the continent and emboldening Kremlin chief Vladimir Putin.
“We already have a European security architecture in place — NATO and European Union both have their respective roles,” EU foreign policy chief Kaja Kallas said Friday in reaction to the U.S. plan. “We must make sure Ukraine is integrated into this architecture. The problem remains that Russia keeps breaking the treaties that underpin it ... Putin does not have a veto over European security.”
The latest U.S. proposal underscores growing anxiety around Trump’s fresh rapprochement with Russia as he ramps up pressure on Ukraine and his administration attempts to revive long-stalled talks to end Moscow’s full-scale war against Kyiv.
POLITICO spoke to 12 NATO diplomats, EU envoys and European government officials, all of whom were granted anonymity to speak freely on the sensitive issue. NATO allies were not briefed about the American plans in advance, according to three alliance diplomats, and many remain skeptical of the idea.
U.S. President Donald Trump late Thursday talked of a “big, beautiful agreement,” after meeting with Putin’s envoy Kirill Dmitriev, adding: “It’s going to involve more than Ukraine, and I could even say it might involve all of Europe.”
“Our objective is to develop practical arrangements that address the security concerns of all sides, reduce the risk of future conflict, and create a more stable and predictable security environment,” Trump’s son-in-law and envoy Jared Kushner added soon after.
Kushner said the arrangement would have five goals: “Permanent security consultations, reliable crisis communications, greater military transparency, reciprocal measures to reduce escalation risks, and an enduring framework for long-term European security and stability.”
“It is a bit obscure what Kushner meant,” said one NATO diplomat. “The general sentiment in Europe is that any discussion with Russia on the future architecture at the moment will just be used by Moscow to legitimize their arguments ... it will not fly with the European allies.”
A senior European official added: “Literally, there’s nothing to find fault with, but we know there’s something else going on.”
European Commission President Ursula von der Leyen’s top adviser, Björn Seibert, briefed EU ambassadors on Friday, according to two EU diplomats, following a discussion between national security advisers on the issue.
“There’s willingness to engage in Kyiv and in the rest of Europe although there’s little confidence in the Russians — but the EU is not blocking it,” one of the EU diplomats said after the meeting. But “the group around Trump underestimated how important the conflict is for Europe and how a bad outcome for Ukraine is very dangerous for Europe.”
“It's a long-standing position for us and many others that European security architecture should not be discussed while there is a war,” said a senior European security official. “And obviously not without Europeans.”
“Europe must have a seat at the table in negotiations on peace in Ukraine and the future European security architecture,” Lithuanian President Gitanas Nausėda added Friday, after a meeting of the eight Nordic and Baltic countries.
This week saw two rounds of working-level meetings in Brussels on a Ukraine peace deal, ahead of U.S.-brokered working-level talks with Ukraine and Russia on Nov. 10-11 in Abu Dhabi.
“We must be realistic about the peace talks and we must be very careful when it comes to the real intentions of Russia,” Polish Prime Minister Donald Tusk told a group of reporters, including from POLITICO, earlier this week. “In winter, Putin might have less incentives to get a deal.”
Stefan Kornelius, spokesperson for German Chancellor Friedrich Merz — who talked to Trump on Thursday night — said: “A new sense of urgency has ... emerged” on negotiations after this week's U.S. midterm elections, adding the issue would resurface at an informal gathering of EU leaders in Dublin next week.
The meeting had been intended to focus on AI, but developments in Ukraine could overshadow the talks, a third EU diplomat said. “Things are moving pretty fast,” they said.
Still, some allies fear the U.S. may tie its new initiative to an upcoming review of American troops in Europe, expected in December.
“That’s the elephant in the room,” said a second NATO diplomat. “One thing is talking about European security architecture ... with an ‘ordinary’ U.S. posture; another thing is to talk about a European security architecture ‘as things will be,’ and nobody knows how that’ll be.”

articles.title_orig: Stock market today: Nasdaq futures rebound after brutal sell-off, Dow and S&P 500 wobble as US adds 165K jobs
articles.title_zh: Stock market today: Nasdaq futures rebound after brutal sell-off, Dow and S&P 500 wobble as US adds 165K jobs
articles.content_orig:
Oops, something went wrong
US stocks stabilized on Friday after a post-election rally turned into an artificial intelligence trade meltdown, sending tremors through markets. Investors also assessed a hotter-than-expected October jobs report.
The Dow Jones Industrial Average ( ^DJI ) rose 0.1%, while the S&P 500 ( ^GSPC ) rose 1%. The Nasdaq Composite ( ^IXIC ) gained 1.9% after the tech-heavy index slipped into a correction on Thursday.
The major indexes were on track to post substantial losses during the volatile election week that saw the Democrats retake the House and Senate . At the center of Thursday's deep sell-off, which erased $2.3 trillion in market value, were concerns about a slowdown in data center construction and in AI spending.
The hit chip stocks like Nvidia ( NVDA ), Micron ( MU ), AMD ( AMD ), and Sandisk ( SNDK ) most directly, but also spilled into broader markets, sending the VIX Volatility Index ( ^VIX ) up 70% to 28.
Oil prices have also been in play, with global benchmark Brent crude ( BZ=F ) and WTI crude ( CL=F ) futures falling below $100 per barrel. Energy traders continue to assess the outlook for the war in the Middle East, with the potential for a reescalation weighing on sentiment.
Not to be overshadowed, the Labor Department reported that the US added 165,000 jobs in October , above a revised 60,000 figure the month before and the 65,000 jobs economists expected.
Chip stocks rebounded on Friday after suffering their worst sell-off since 2020. The PHLX Semiconductor Index ( ^SOX ) bounced 4% following a 12% plunge on Thursday.
Shares of US chipmaker Intel ( INTC ) jumped nearly 6%, erasing part of their 10% slide in the prior session. AMD ( AMD ) also rebounded 8% after suffering a 17% fall. Nvidia ( NVDA ), which declined 9% in the prior session, jumped 6%.
Semiconductors bounced back after much of the AI trade was hammered on Thursday as investors digested what a Democratic win in Congress means for the data center build-out in the US.
Memory and storage names Sandisk ( SNDK ), Micron Technology ( MU ) and SK Hynix ( SKHY ) shares tumbled alongside Samsung Electronics ( 005930.KS ) following Thursday's wipeout on Wall Street.
US stocks were mixed at Friday's open as investors looked for more signs that market conditions have stabilized after Thursday's sharp AI-led sell-off.
The Dow Jones Industrial Average ( ^DJI ) fell 0.9%, while the S&P 500 ( ^GSPC ) rose 0.4%. The tech-heavy Nasdaq Composite ( ^IXIC ) rose more than 1.4%.
Technology shares attempted to rebound after Thursday's rout, which pushed the Nasdaq back into correction territory and erased much of Wednesday's post-election rally.
Investors were also parsing the October jobs report for clues on whether the labor market remains strong enough to keep another Federal Reserve rate hike in play.
Yahoo Finance's Jennifer Schonberger reports:
A much stronger-than-expected October jobs report solidifies expectations that the Federal Reserve will raise interest rates in December, as officials are already focused on higher inflation.
The Bureau of Labor Statistics report released Friday showed that 165,000 jobs were created in October , compared with expectations for around 70,000, as the unemployment rate edged down to 4.1%, compared with expectations for 4.2%. That's much higher than the average monthly gain of 48,000 over the past 12 months and well above the roughly 30,000 jobs needed to hold employment steady. Labor force participation inched up to a hair above expectations at 61.9%.
Job gains in both August and September were also revised higher by 84,000. The bulk of jobs added were in the sectors of professional and business services, healthcare, and transportation and warehousing. Manufacturing added 19,000 jobs.
The US economy added 165,000 jobs in October, a jump from the revised job growth of 60,000 the month before. Economists surveyed by Bloomberg expected the economy to have added 65,000 jobs.
The unemployment rate ticked down to 4.1%. Wage growth increased 0.4% from September.
If you are looking for something positive after Thursday's shocking stock beatdown , you have come to the right place ahead of the weekend.
History suggests stocks tend to do well after the extreme volatility we saw two days removed from the Election Day blue wave.
The VIX volatility index ( ^VVIX ) — better known as Wall Street's fear gauge — jumped as much as 70% on Thursday. A move this large has only happened eight times since 1991, according to data from CBOE.
Here's what happened to the S&P 500 on average after the eight prior extreme moves:
1 month later: +3.0% (7 of 8 times positive)
3 months later: +7.1% (6 of 8 times positive)
6 months later: +10.4% (8 of 8 times positive)
1 year later: +14.7% (7 of 8 times positive)
The stock market's Thursday rout in artificial intelligence boom trade may have been an overreaction to growing political opposition to data center construction, according to one prominent bull.
AI and chip stocks plunged Thursday as major indexes erased their post-midterm election rally. One key worry is that about 45% of planned US data center capacity faces possible restrictions after tallying newly elected state governors who have promised to stop or pause construction, according to Goldman Sachs estimates.
But Yardeni Research is calling those mounting restrictions a setback.
"We view the political backlash as another constraint on AI investment, alongside financial and physical bottlenecks. But these are speed bumps, not roadblocks, even though Wall Street seems to be pricing in the latter," Yardeni Research wrote in a Friday note to clients.
"We think that's overdone," the strategists said, referring to Thursday's sell-off as a "buying opportunity." The firm is sticking with its year-end target of 7,900 on the S&P 500.
Yardeni pointed to Texas, a major data center hub, where newly elected governor Gina Hinojosa said Thursday afternoon in a CNN interview that already permitted projects would be allowed to finish construction.
The distinction matters. Permitted data center projects account for "essentially all of Texas's planned data center capacity in 2027 and likely much of 2028," according to Yardeni.
Employment data scheduled for release on Friday is expected to show the labor market remains steady. Yahoo Finance's Claire Boston previews what to expect from today's jobs report:
Economists surveyed by Bloomberg expect that the economy added 65,000 jobs in October, an improvement from September's underwhelming 29,000 additions. The unemployment rate is expected to hold steady at 4.2%, while wage growth is seen improving 0.3% from September.
Those numbers would be consistent with the "low hire, low fire" environment that has defined the labor market for the past several years. While few companies are hiring aggressively, most aren't conducting major layoffs either.
Recent initial jobless claims have looked "exceptionally benign by historical standards," Bank of America economist Shruti Mishra wrote in a note.
"Despite recent high-profile layoff announcements, the absence of any pickup in claims suggests economy-wide layoffs remain contained," she added.
Yahoo Finance's Hamza Shaban writes:
When President Trump and his allies in Congress moved to end the EV subsidy, automakers braced for a crash in electric car sales. Tesla ( TSLA ), the US leader, was especially vulnerable because it didn't have gas-powered vehicles to lean on, and keeping prices as low as possible was crucial to competing with EV rivals.
But those initial worries gave way to optimism.

It lost a valuable subsidy, but used its scale to win a war of attrition, thereby consolidating the market.
